$DELL KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM DELL TECHNOLOGIES Q2 FY2027 EARNINGS CALL

Dell Technologies’ Q2 FY2027 call provides unusually strong confirmation that the current data-center capital-spending cycle is broadening beyond GPU purchases into a much larger infrastructure refresh encompassing CPU servers, memory, storage, networking, optics, power, cooling, and enterprise PCs. The most important cross-market signal is that AI demand is increasingly additive to, rather than cannibalistic of, traditional infrastructure spending. Dell booked $60.9B of AI server orders in a single quarter, exited with $95B of AI backlog, and nevertheless generated 122% growth in traditional servers and networking and 26% growth in storage. Demand exceeded supply in both AI and conventional infrastructure. Management explicitly identified DRAM and NAND as the most acute shortages, followed by CPUs, disk drives, optics, substrates, power semiconductors, cooling distribution units, and power racks. The call therefore supports a broader and more durable AI infrastructure spending thesis than one centered solely on accelerators.

A second important read-through is that enterprise AI adoption appears to be inflecting. Dell’s AI customer count surpassed 6,500, with approximately 3,300 customers added during the last 3 quarters versus approximately 3,200 accumulated during the preceding 8 quarters. Enterprise customers, repeat buyers, enterprise AI revenue, and enterprise pipeline all increased. Enterprise AI customers also purchase more storage and networking, making the enterprise mix disproportionately important for suppliers outside the GPU complex. At the same time, Dell reported more than 10 points of traditional-server share gain over 2 quarters, introducing material competitive implications for competing server OEMs even as the overall market expands.

The highest-conviction read-throughs are positive for NVIDIA, memory suppliers, data-center power and thermal infrastructure companies, storage vendors exposed to unstructured AI data, CPU suppliers, and selected networking/optical vendors. The principal negative read-throughs are relative rather than absolute: competing server OEMs face evidence of Dell share gains; PC manufacturers face persistent memory inflation and less pricing power than data-center vendors; and storage vendors face increasingly aggressive competition from Dell as Dell-IP products regain share.

AI ACCELERATORS AND COMPUTE

NVIDIA — DEMAND VISIBILITY EXTENDS WELL BEYOND CURRENT SHIPMENTS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected Company: NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA: US)

Directional Impact: POSITIVE

Magnitude: VERY HIGH

Time Horizon: Near-term trading catalyst and long-duration fundamental positive.

Dell’s AI server metrics provide one of the strongest independent demand confirmations for NVIDIA’s accelerator roadmap. Dell booked $60.9B of AI server orders during Q2, recognized only $16.4B of AI server revenue, and exited with $95B of backlog. Orders were approximately 3.7x quarterly revenue, while backlog was approximately 5.8x quarterly AI server revenue.

The most important point is the order-to-revenue divergence. Dell’s AI server revenue increased only modestly sequentially, but orders exploded. This implies that demand creation is occurring considerably faster than hardware can currently be supplied and deployed.

Management stated that Dell has booked more than $130B of AI server orders during the past 12 months and that the forward pipeline continued to grow sequentially despite this extraordinary order conversion. Management also said the pipeline remained “multiples of our backlog.”

The transmission mechanism to NVIDIA is direct. Dell’s AI infrastructure franchise is heavily centered on NVIDIA accelerator platforms, with Dell participating in successive NVIDIA architecture transitions and specifically discussing Vera Rubin deployment capabilities. Dell’s $95B backlog therefore represents substantial future accelerator, networking, memory, and system content that has been ordered at the OEM level but not yet recognized as Dell revenue.

The call also substantially reduces the risk that NVIDIA’s growth is dependent exclusively on a handful of hyperscalers. Dell reported growing AI demand from neoclouds, sovereign customers, high-frequency trading customers, and enterprises. The AI customer count exceeded 6,500.

Enterprise adoption appears particularly important. Dell said:

“3,300 of them have happened in the last three quarters. It took us eight quarters to get to the first 3,200.”

This indicates a major acceleration in the breadth of AI infrastructure adoption.

The longer-duration implication is positive because Dell views inference, rather than training alone, as the increasingly important demand driver. Management argued that inference token volumes could increase dramatically through 2030 and that enterprise agentic workloads will become a major source of infrastructure demand.

Inference is particularly attractive for NVIDIA because it increases the utilization of the installed accelerator base while simultaneously driving continued demand for new hardware generations optimized around performance per watt and token economics.

The largest risk to interpreting Dell’s backlog as NVIDIA revenue is timing rather than demand. Power availability, memory supply, cooling infrastructure, customer facility readiness, and component constraints can delay system shipment. Dell’s commentary therefore argues for strong NVIDIA demand visibility while also reinforcing the possibility that quarterly accelerator shipment timing remains volatile.

The near-term trading implication is strongly positive. Dell’s order acceleration suggests that the Vera Rubin cycle is entering with exceptionally strong downstream OEM demand rather than requiring a new demand-generation phase.

The longer-duration fundamental implication is even more important: AI compute demand appears to be broadening from hyperscale training toward sovereign, neocloud, HFT, and enterprise inference workloads, materially increasing the breadth of NVIDIA’s end-market exposure.

MEMORY SEMICONDUCTORS

DRAM AND NAND HAVE BECOME SYSTEM-LEVEL BOTTLENECKS — STRONG POSITIVE FOR MEMORY PRICING (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected Companies:

Micron Technology (MU: US)

SK hynix (000660: South Korea)

Samsung Electronics (005930: South Korea)

Directional Impact: POSITIVE

Magnitude: VERY HIGH

Time Horizon: Strong near-term pricing catalyst and positive medium-duration industry-cycle read-through.

Dell provided an unusually explicit confirmation that memory has become the most important broad-based supply bottleneck across enterprise computing.

Management described the supply hierarchy as:

“DRAM, DRAM, DRAM, followed by NAND, NAND, NAND.”

This was not restricted to AI systems. Dell indicated that conventional server configurations are increasingly memory intensive because modernization involves higher core counts, greater DRAM capacity, and more local storage.

Traditional server and networking revenue increased 122% in Q2, while Dell still stated that demand materially exceeded supply.

This creates 3 simultaneous memory demand vectors.

The 1st is AI infrastructure. AI servers require enormous quantities of HBM, conventional DRAM, NAND, and supporting storage.

The 2nd is conventional server modernization. New systems are being configured with significantly more DRAM per node as customers consolidate older server estates.

The 3rd is AI-driven CPU infrastructure. Agentic AI requires traditional CPU servers for orchestration, retrieval, application execution, scheduling, state management, databases, and other workloads surrounding accelerator clusters.

This means the current memory cycle is not merely an HBM cycle. Increasing HBM production can constrain conventional DRAM wafer allocation while conventional server and PC demand simultaneously requires additional DRAM.

For Micron, SK hynix, and Samsung, this materially improves pricing power across memory categories.

The near-term implication is higher contract DRAM pricing, higher NAND pricing, favorable utilization, and limited customer ability to defer purchases where systems are already ordered.

Dell’s ability to pass increased component costs through to customers strengthens the supplier read-through. Management explicitly said traditional servers:

“cost more than they did last quarter and the quarter before and the quarter before.”

Dell nevertheless reported demand exceeding available supply.

This is economically significant because it indicates that memory inflation has not yet materially impaired data-center demand elasticity.

SK hynix remains particularly exposed to the AI-memory supercycle through HBM leadership.

Micron benefits from both HBM and conventional DRAM/NAND tightness.

Samsung has comparatively broader memory exposure and therefore benefits strongly if conventional DRAM and NAND pricing remains elevated alongside AI demand.

The medium-term risk is eventual capacity response. However, Dell’s commentary suggests that memory tightness is currently being reinforced by simultaneous AI, enterprise-server, storage, and PC requirements rather than a narrow single-product shortage.

The highest-conviction implication is therefore that the current memory upcycle has greater breadth and potentially greater duration than a conventional inventory-driven semiconductor cycle.

DATA-CENTER POWER AND THERMAL INFRASTRUCTURE

DELL CONFIRMS THAT ELECTRICAL AND COOLING INFRASTRUCTURE IS OPERATING AT MAXIMUM INDUSTRY CAPACITY (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected Companies:

Vertiv Holdings (VRT: US)

Eaton Corporation (ETN: US)

Schneider Electric (SU: France)

Directional Impact: POSITIVE

Magnitude: VERY HIGH

Time Horizon: Strong near-term demand confirmation and major long-duration structural positive.

Dell’s commentary provides a highly constructive read-through for the electrical and thermal infrastructure ecosystem.

Management stated:

“The AI supply chain is working red line all out to build CDUs, power racks.”

The significance is greater than a simple component shortage. AI server systems increasingly require liquid cooling, high-voltage power distribution, rack-level power architecture, UPS infrastructure, switchgear, transformers, busway, and sophisticated thermal management.

Dell also cited a potential requirement for approximately 200 GW of incremental data-center power through 2030.

Even allowing for substantial uncertainty around that estimate, Dell’s $95B backlog demonstrates that server demand is already materially ahead of the physical infrastructure required to deploy it.

Vertiv is one of the clearest beneficiaries because high-density AI racks require liquid cooling, coolant distribution units, thermal-management systems, power distribution, and integrated data-center infrastructure. The transition from conventional air-cooled racks toward liquid-cooled accelerated computing materially increases Vertiv content per MW.

Eaton benefits further upstream from electrical distribution requirements including switchgear, UPS systems, busway, breakers, power-management systems, and broader data-center electrical infrastructure.

Schneider Electric similarly benefits across low- and medium-voltage electrical systems, power distribution, UPS, data-center management, and cooling.

The transmission mechanism is exceptionally strong because electrical and cooling infrastructure must generally be installed before Dell can convert much of its AI backlog into revenue. Dell’s inability to monetize server orders without completed customer infrastructure effectively makes power and cooling investment a prerequisite for monetizing already-booked compute demand.

This reduces the degree to which power-equipment demand is dependent on speculative future AI forecasts. A meaningful amount is associated with infrastructure already ordered downstream.

The near-term catalyst is continued backlog expansion and pricing power across power and cooling equipment.

The longer-duration shift is more important. Rack densities continue rising with successive GPU generations, causing power and cooling content per rack to increase even if GPU unit growth eventually slows.

A migration from tens of kilowatts per rack toward 100+ kW and increasingly higher densities creates a structural increase in thermal and power-system content.

For Vertiv, Eaton, and Schneider, Dell’s commentary reinforces the thesis that the limiting factor in AI deployment is increasingly physical infrastructure rather than demand for compute.

ENTERPRISE SERVER CPUs

THE AI BOOM IS CREATING A SECOND COMPUTE CYCLE IN CPUs, NOT ONLY GPUs (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected Companies:

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD: US)

Intel Corporation (INTC: US)

Directional Impact: POSITIVE

Magnitude: HIGH

Time Horizon: Medium-term fundamental positive.

Dell’s 122% growth in traditional servers and networking is a major read-through for server CPU demand.

The initial assumption that accelerated computing would cannibalize conventional CPU server budgets appears increasingly incorrect. Dell reported the opposite.

Management identified 2 major sources of traditional server demand: modernization of aged enterprise infrastructure and incremental CPU workloads created by AI.

The AI-specific mechanism is particularly important.

Management said customers require:

“meaningful CPU compute capacity to support AI and agentic workflows.”

Agentic AI requires substantial CPU resources outside GPU inference itself. These workloads include orchestration, application execution, databases, retrieval, vector manipulation, security, scheduling, middleware, data preparation, storage management, and communication between agents and enterprise systems.

This creates a complementary relationship between CPUs and GPUs.

The strongest immediate beneficiary is AMD because additional enterprise server deployments create incremental EPYC demand, while AMD simultaneously participates in accelerator opportunities through Instinct.

Intel also benefits because Dell’s installed enterprise base remains extremely large and Xeon continues to have substantial enterprise presence.

Dell cited approximately 1.2M servers in its installed base that are 14G or older.

The hardware-refresh opportunity is therefore substantial even before incremental AI workloads are considered.

There is an important offset: new servers can consolidate multiple older servers. Dell discussed consolidation ratios of approximately 6-8 old systems into a new 17G server and potentially 12-14 older systems into an 18G system.

Therefore, CPU unit demand does not increase proportionally with retired-server counts.

However, newer servers have higher core counts and substantially higher silicon, DRAM, storage, and networking content.

The economic read-through for AMD and Intel is consequently better measured in CPU dollars and compute capacity than physical socket count.

The longer-duration non-consensus implication is that agentic AI may materially expand the total CPU addressable market even as GPUs capture a larger proportion of total data-center silicon spending.

This is particularly relevant for AMD because market-share gains in general-purpose server CPUs can coexist with continued AI accelerator growth rather than being crowded out by it.

ENTERPRISE SERVER OEMS

DELL’S >10-POINT SERVER SHARE GAIN IS A MATERIAL COMPETITIVE WARNING FOR HPE AND LENOVO (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected Companies:

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE: US)

Lenovo Group (0992: Hong Kong/China)

Directional Impact: NEGATIVE RELATIVE READ-THROUGH

Magnitude: MEDIUM-HIGH

Time Horizon: Near-term competitive negative with longer-duration share implications.

Dell stated that it gained more than 10 points of traditional server share over the last 2 quarters and expects additional share gains.

This is one of the strongest competitive signals in the call.

Traditional server and networking revenue increased 122%, meaning Dell is not merely gaining share in a contracting or stagnant market. It is capturing an outsized portion of an accelerating enterprise refresh cycle.

The primary competitive exposure falls on HPE and Lenovo, which overlap materially with Dell in enterprise x86 infrastructure.

The transmission mechanism is straightforward. Enterprise server customers typically maintain multi-vendor procurement frameworks, and incremental Dell share generally comes at the expense of competing OEM allocations.

Dell’s advantage appears to derive from supply-chain execution, pricing, breadth of product, enterprise relationships, financing, and the ability to bundle servers with storage, networking, deployment, and AI infrastructure.

Dell’s statement that demand exceeded supply also implies its share gains were not achieved through aggressive discounting alone.

Q2 ISG operating margin reached 15%, indicating that Dell simultaneously gained share and expanded profitability.

That makes the competitive signal materially more adverse.

For HPE, the offset is that the overall market is growing dramatically and HPE has meaningful AI, networking, and liquid-cooling exposure. Absolute HPE server revenue can therefore increase while Dell still takes share.

The implication is more negative for relative growth and incremental margins than for absolute industry demand.

For Lenovo, the same broad TAM benefit exists, but Dell’s strength in large US enterprise accounts creates a particularly relevant competitive read-through.

A notable long-duration risk is that AI deepens vendor consolidation. Enterprise customers deploying Dell AI infrastructure may increasingly purchase Dell traditional servers, storage, networking, and PCs around the same environment.

Dell explicitly said enterprise AI customers:

“tend to buy more storage and they tend to buy more networking when they engage with us, a more complete solution.”

If this cross-selling behavior persists, AI deployments could become a customer-acquisition and share-consolidation mechanism across infrastructure categories rather than a standalone server transaction.

This creates a longer-duration competitive threat for vendors lacking comparable portfolio breadth.

SUPERMICRO

DELL’S SCALE ADVANTAGE IS BECOMING MORE VALUABLE AS AI SYSTEM COMPLEXITY INCREASES (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected Company: Super Micro Computer (SMCI: US)

Directional Impact: MIXED, WITH A NEGATIVE RELATIVE-COMPETITIVE SIGNAL

Magnitude: MEDIUM

Time Horizon: Longer-duration competitive read-through.

Dell’s AI demand is positive for the overall server ecosystem and therefore validates Supermicro’s end market. However, the call contains an increasingly important negative competitive implication for smaller AI-focused system integrators.

Dell emphasized that AI infrastructure is becoming substantially more complicated than assembling accelerator boards into servers.

Management described some engagements as requiring:

“upwards of 50 unique designs”

to address workload performance, power, cooling, and physical data-center requirements.

Dell then emphasized engineering, global deployment, supply-chain scale, service capabilities, and financing as differentiators.

As AI deployment moves from standardized hyperscale clusters toward sovereign and enterprise customers, these capabilities become increasingly important.

Large enterprises often require global service contracts, financing, validated architectures, lifecycle support, storage integration, data protection, networking, security certification, and deployment services.

This structurally favors Dell relative to narrower system assemblers.

Supermicro remains a major beneficiary of overall accelerated-computing growth and has important strengths in rapid platform deployment and liquid-cooled architectures. The read-through is therefore not fundamentally bearish for Supermicro revenue.

The negative implication is relative competitive positioning.

Dell’s AI customer count has exceeded 6,500, enterprise customer additions are accelerating, and Dell has access to a very large installed enterprise account base.

If the next phase of AI adoption shifts toward mainstream enterprise deployment, Dell’s distribution and services advantages become more powerful.

The market could consequently become less commoditized at the system-assembly layer as customers place greater value on integrated deployment and support.

This argues against assuming that all AI server OEMs will maintain similar growth or margin trajectories as the customer mix broadens.

DATA-CENTER STORAGE

AI STORAGE IS MOVING FROM A SECONDARY BENEFICIARY TO A CORE INFRASTRUCTURE REQUIREMENT (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected Companies:

NetApp (NTAP: US)

Pure Storage (PSTG: US)

Western Digital (WDC: US)

Seagate Technology (STX: US)

Directional Impact: POSITIVE INDUSTRY READ-THROUGH

Magnitude: HIGH

Time Horizon: Medium- and long-duration fundamental positive.

Dell’s 26% storage growth is important because it provides evidence that AI infrastructure spending is beginning to pull storage demand higher rather than simply consuming compute budgets.

Dell cited increasing AI requirements around data preparation, management, movement, protection, unstructured data, key-value cache, and agentic workflows.

Management described the underlying dynamic:

“more data is being created on the planet, at the edge, in data centers, in the cloud, and that data has to be stored, it has to be encrypted and protected.”

AI compounds this requirement because enterprise inference requires persistent access to proprietary datasets rather than only temporary training data.

Agentic applications generate additional logs, vectors, context, outputs, intermediate states, and retained records.

Management also highlighted retention requirements associated with AI outputs and agent activity.

Physical AI represents another long-duration driver because robotics, autonomous systems, industrial sensors, video, and multimodal applications produce enormous quantities of unstructured data.

This is directly positive for Pure Storage and NetApp because high-performance enterprise AI workloads require low-latency scalable storage, data management, hybrid-cloud integration, and increasingly sophisticated software.

The call is particularly supportive of the thesis that AI storage opportunity extends beyond a small number of training clusters. Enterprise inference creates a much broader installed-base opportunity.

For Seagate and Western Digital, the read-through is positive through mass-capacity storage and unstructured data growth. Dell specifically cited disk-drive shortages within the supply chain.

AI does not eliminate HDD demand because the lowest-cost tier for very large datasets, model archives, backup, retention, object repositories, and data lakes continues to favor high-capacity disk.

The key longer-duration implication is that AI increases the value of data persistence.

Compute can be replaced or rented, but enterprise proprietary data is durable and continuously expanding. This supports storage spending through multiple AI hardware cycles.

VOL TERM STRUCTURE TREND — 6 MONTHS
The 360D ATM IV series is the closest available proxy for the long-dated vol trend (historical data for the specific Jan 2028 option contracts is not available). The key takeaway: long-end vol has compressed sharply across most names since the March–June peak, tracking the front-end crush but with meaningfully less magnitude — the curve has flattened.
•NVDA: 360D IV has declined from ~50%+ in the April–May stress period to 38.3% today. The 30D/360D spread has compressed to just 6 ppts — the curve is historically flat, meaning the long end is cheap in absolute terms but the term premium is thin.
•AMD: 360D IV peaked near 70% in late May/early June and has since fallen to 55.2%. Front-end compressed harder (-10% 30D change vs. -14% at 360D), so the curve has actually steepened slightly — long-end vol is holding up better than short-end.
•AVGO: The notable outlier — 30D IV (50.5%) sits above 360D IV (46.6%), an inverted term structure. This reflects residual near-term event premium (likely post-earnings positioning) rather than structural long-end richness. The Jan 2028 0.35Δ call at 47.6% is essentially at-or-below the 360D ATM level — relatively attractive on a term structure basis.
•MRVL: Long-end vol has actually risen over the past 6 months — 360D IV up ~18% from March levels to 65.6%. The Jan 2028 call at 69.0% reflects this. MRVL is the most expensive name in the group on a long-dated basis, and the recent -12% spot move this week has not yet fully resolved.
•CEG / GEV: Both at 1Y IV rank lows. 360D IV for CEG at 43.2% and GEV at 49.9% — these are near multi-year lows for long-dated power/energy infrastructure vol. The Jan 2028 calls are priced close to the 360D ATM level, suggesting the market is not pricing in meaningful incremental uncertainty beyond 1 year.
•SMCI: Highest absolute IV in the group at 79.6%, but the long-end premium over 30D is only 1.5 ppts — the curve is nearly flat. Long-dated vol is expensive in absolute terms but not in relative term-structure terms.
ATTRACTIVENESS OF LONG-DATED CALLS — FRAMEWORK
The vol-down environment creates a mixed setup for LEAPS buyers. The key variables are: (1) absolute IV level vs. expected realized vol over the holding period, (2) term structure shape (steep = long-end relatively cheap; inverted = near-term event premium you’re overpaying for), and (3) IV rank at the long end specifically.
Bottom line: NVDA and CEG screen as the most attractive LEAPS candidates on a vol basis — long-dated IV near 1-year lows, normal term structures, and post-catalyst vol crush complete. AVGO is worth a closer look given the inverted curve (near-term event premium you avoid by going long-dated). MRVL and SMCI are expensive on a long-dated basis despite the broader vol-down environment.

$CLMT CALUMET MAXSAF EXPANSION: INVESTMENT ANALYSIS

EXECUTIVE ASSESSMENT

Calumet’s revised MaxSAF expansion is materially positive for the probability-weighted value of Montana Renewables and Calumet equity. The principal value creation comes from eliminating a major financing, dilution, and construction overhang rather than from creating an entirely incremental 200 million-gallon earnings stream.

The remaining project capital requirement falls to $137 million from the $1.2 billion contemplated under the original Phase 2 plan. Remaining DOE funding declines from as much as $658 million to a final $34 million draw, while approximately $103 million is expected to be funded from Montana Renewables retained earnings. The revised structure eliminates the prior requirement for approximately $538 million of 3rd-party equity, preserving Calumet’s ownership and avoiding a materially more complex capital structure.

The project retains approximately 200 million gallons of annual SAF capacity versus the original approximately 300 million-gallon SAF target. It therefore preserves approximately 66.7 percent of original SAF nameplate capacity while reducing stated remaining capital by approximately 88.6 percent. This is a substantial improvement in capital efficiency and execution risk, although the comparison does not fully capture deleted hydrogen, water-treatment, cogeneration, logistics, blending, and other infrastructure.

The revised plan is best understood as a capital-allocation and risk-reset event:

* Financing risk declines sharply.
* Expected dilution is eliminated.
* Future DOE debt and cash-sweep burdens are reduced.
* Construction changes from 1 megaproject to 6 smaller modules.
* Brownfield equipment reuse lowers procurement and field-construction risk.
* Absolute upside is reduced relative to a successful 300 million-gallon project.
* Operating, feedstock, policy, and product-netback risks become the dominant variables.

The 200 million-gallon SAF target is not equivalent to 200 million gallons of incremental production. Current SAF output is approximately 60 million gallons on an annualized run-rate basis. Total product sales are expected to increase from approximately 12,000 barrels per day to approximately 17,000 barrels per day, equal to approximately 76.7 million incremental annual saleable gallons. SAF production increases by approximately 140 million gallons, indicating that a substantial portion of growth reflects conversion of existing renewable diesel into higher-value SAF rather than purely incremental throughput.

The core recurring economic variable is therefore the incremental netback of SAF versus renewable diesel after hydrogen, catalyst, fractionation, yield loss, logistics, blending, and commercial costs. Gross SAF volume alone is not an adequate measure of value creation.

CAPITAL EFFICIENCY

Key capital metrics include:

* $137 million equals approximately 11.4 percent of the original $1.2 billion Phase 2 estimate.
* The $1.063 billion reduction in stated capital equals approximately 88.6 percent.
* The $624 million reduction in remaining DOE availability equals approximately 94.8 percent.
* Remaining capital equals approximately $0.98 per incremental annual SAF gallon when measured against the increase from 60 million to 200 million gallons.
* Remaining capital equals approximately $1.79 per incremental annual saleable gallon when measured against total product-sales growth.

Management’s statement that approximately 70 percent of the original benefit is retained for approximately 15 percent of original capital is directionally plausible but not fully reconciled. The 70 percent claim broadly matches the 200 million-gallon revised SAF target relative to the original 300 million-gallon target. However, $137 million is only approximately 11.4 percent of $1.2 billion. The difference may reflect capital already incurred, but complete reconciliation requires disclosure of spending to date, stage-level budgets, contingencies, capitalized turnaround costs, and costs embedded in the CMR lease.

The $137 million headline also may not represent total economic capital. Potential exclusions include the present value of CMR lease payments, refurbishment, foregone CMR contribution, decommissioning, owner’s costs, contingencies, working capital, replacement utilities, and lender-consent or environmental costs.

PAYBACK SENSITIVITY

The remaining capital is sufficiently low that moderate operating uplift could generate attractive returns:

* A 2-year simple payback requires approximately $68.5 million of annual incremental EBITDA.
* A 3-year payback requires approximately $45.7 million.
* A 4-year payback requires approximately $34.3 million.
* A 5-year payback requires approximately $27.4 million.

Measured against the 140 million-gallon increase in annual SAF output, the required contribution is approximately $0.49 per gallon for a 2-year payback, $0.33 for 3 years, $0.24 for 4 years, and $0.20 for 5 years.

Renewable propane and butane recovery, improved renewable naphtha yield, lower water usage, and lower unit costs reduce the SAF premium required. However, low capital intensity does not protect against negative operating spreads because annual feedstock expenditures will be many multiples of the expansion budget.

PRODUCTION RAMP AND PRODUCT MIX

The disclosed SAF trajectory is:

* Current run rate: approximately 60 million gallons.
* Year-end 2026: more than 80 million gallons.
* Spring 2027: more than 120 million gallons.
* During 2027: approximately 120 million to 150 million gallons.
* Year-end 2028: approximately 200 million gallons.

These are run-rate targets rather than annual production volumes. Full-year target economics would begin in 2029, subject to successful commissioning and stable utilization.

At the 2028 target:

* 200 million gallons of SAF equal approximately 13,000 barrels per day.
* Total product sales of approximately 17,000 barrels per day equal approximately 260.6 million gallons annually.
* SAF would represent approximately 76.7 percent of saleable volume.
* Approximately 20 million gallons of renewable propane and butane would equal approximately 1,300 barrels per day.
* The remaining approximately 40.6 million gallons would consist primarily of renewable diesel and renewable naphtha.

Current renewable diesel plus SAF production is approximately 11,000 to 12,000 barrels per day, while current SAF production is approximately 3,900 barrels per day. This implies approximately 7,000 to 8,000 barrels per day of current renewable diesel production. At the target, renewable diesel plus SAF production is approximately 14,000 to 15,000 barrels per day, with SAF representing approximately 13,000 barrels per day. The plan therefore appears to convert approximately 5,000 to 7,000 barrels per day of renewable diesel into SAF while adding approximately 3,000 barrels per day of combined renewable diesel and SAF throughput.

This confirms that the SAF-versus-renewable-diesel margin differential is more important than gross SAF sales value.

TECHNICAL CONFIGURATION

The centerpiece is the long-term lease and integration of a CMR hydrotreater, hydrogen plant, and naphtha splitter. The tied-in hydrotreater will operate as a polishing reactor rather than a conventional severe cracking reactor. Intended benefits include higher SAF recovery, less overcracking into light products, lower liquid yield loss, reduced by-product production, and improved catalyst and severity management.

The concept is technically credible, but the economic advantage remains unverified because no quantitative yield data have been disclosed. Required diligence includes current and target SAF yield, renewable diesel yield, renewable naphtha yield, renewable LPG yield, hydrogen consumption, catalyst life, product loss, feedstock-specific performance, and achieved jet-fuel specifications.

The 6-project structure includes spring 2026 constraint removal, the CMR equipment tie-in, off-gas handling and renewable LPG recovery, water and feedstock-selectivity improvements, fractionation modifications, and hydrogen-supply expansion. Modular construction should lower catastrophic execution risk, but the modules remain operationally interdependent. Hydrogen, utilities, fractionation, water, controls, and turnaround timing could constrain the system if 1 module underperforms.

Brownfield reuse reduces equipment lead time and large-scale construction exposure but introduces risks around equipment condition, metallurgy, prior service, controls integration, piping, compressors, heat integration, maintenance history, permits, and restart reliability.

Hydrogen is a critical constraint. Higher SAF production generally requires greater hydrogen consumption, particularly for lower-quality feedstocks. Hydrogen cost, natural-gas sensitivity, plant reliability, carbon intensity, and maintenance will affect operating margin and Section 45Z value.

RENEWABLE LPG AND NAPHTHA

The project is expected to recover approximately 20 million gallons per year of renewable propane and butane currently burned as fuel gas. This increases saleable volume and reported yield, but gross product value is not EBITDA.

Net contribution equals selling price and environmental attributes less avoided internal fuel value, replacement natural-gas or utility cost, separation, compression, storage, transportation, fractionation, and marketing expense.

Improved renewable naphtha yield could also create incremental physical margin and environmental attributes. Value depends on pathway eligibility, RIN treatment, product specifications, destination, and netback relative to internal use.

CMR RECONFIGURATION

CMR’s FCC and alkylation units are expected to be permanently retired in Q4 2026, while asphalt operations continue. Employees and shared-site efficiencies are expected to be retained.

The approximately $50 million of CMR EBITDA expected before transition reflects currently elevated refining margins and should be treated as temporary. It is not a recurring post-transition contribution and should not be capitalized into terminal value.

The consolidated economic test is whether incremental MRL cash flow exceeds foregone normalized CMR fuels EBITDA, asphalt-only operating costs, lease-related costs, decommissioning, replacement utilities, sustaining capital, and lost refining-cycle optionality.

Intercompany lease income and expense eliminate at the consolidated level, but the opportunity cost of retiring CMR units does not. Lease pricing, duration, maintenance obligations, termination rights, residual value, and lender consents will determine value allocation among the restricted group, DOE creditors, existing MRL minority investors, and Calumet shareholders.

DOE LOAN AMENDMENT

The initial $782 million DOE tranche was funded in February 2025. The final amended draw is approximately $34 million, producing aggregate nominal funded availability of approximately $816 million before capitalized interest.

The loan retains a 15-year tenor, U.S. Treasury rate plus 0.375 percent annual interest, deferred servicing until commissioning, a March 2029 initial servicing date, and December 2039 maturity.

This is exceptionally low-cost capital relative to Calumet’s restricted-group debt. However, interest continues to accrue during construction, and deferred servicing is not interest-free financing.

The amendment is positive because it avoids as much as $624 million of incremental DOE debt, reduces future debt service and cash sweeps, lowers completion and reserve risk, eliminates approximately $538 million of required 3rd-party equity, and preserves strategic flexibility.

The March 2029 servicing date leaves only approximately 3 months between the year-end 2028 production target and initial debt service. Any delay in achieving stable operations would reduce the operating cushion.

SELF-FUNDING AND LIQUIDITY

Approximately $103 million is expected to be funded from MRL retained earnings. This appears feasible but is not assured.

The Montana/Renewables segment reported approximately $10.7 million of cash adjusted EBITDA in Q2 2026 and approximately $26.6 million including estimated tax attributes. H1 cash adjusted EBITDA was approximately negative $1.7 million, while the figure including tax attributes was approximately $36.7 million. A 48-day turnaround distorted these results, and combined segment reporting does not provide a clean standalone measure of MRL cash flow.

Key liquidity constraints include:

* MRL and CMR are reported together, obscuring standalone MRL earnings.
* Unrestricted-subsidiary cash cannot be assumed to be freely distributable.
* Higher throughput will increase feedstock working capital.
* Tax credits, RINs, and product sales settle on different timelines.
* DOE reserves and operating liquidity may limit capital available for construction.
* Retained earnings used for expansion cannot simultaneously be distributed or used to resolve minority interests.

Self-funding avoids dilution but has a real opportunity cost. Weak margins, lower RIN prices, feedstock inflation, or an extended outage could force slower sequencing or additional financing.

BALANCE-SHEET AND OWNERSHIP IMPLICATIONS

Avoiding $624 million of additional DOE borrowing materially reduces consolidated gross debt growth. DOE debt is structurally nonrecourse to the restricted group, but it reduces MRL equity value and distributable cash.

The restricted group retains meaningful 2028 and 2029 maturities, overlapping with MaxSAF completion and the start of DOE servicing. Structural separation reduces direct recourse, but consolidated equity value remains sensitive to successful refinancing and MRL execution.

No new 3rd-party equity is required, but MRL already has a preferred minority investor that contributed $250 million in 2022 for an interest representing approximately 14.2 percent of MRHL. The investor is entitled to the greater of an 8 percent internal rate of return or a specified invested-capital multiple, preferential cash allocation until return thresholds are met, and strategic rights beginning in August 2027 under defined conditions.

Gross MRL enterprise value therefore cannot be attributed directly to Calumet common equity. Adjustments are required for DOE debt, accrued interest, preferred returns, minority ownership, cash sweeps, operating reserves, and lease obligations.

The August 2027 activation of minority strategic rights could catalyze an MRL public offering, sale, recapitalization, or preferred-interest resolution before completion of the full expansion.

SECTION 45Z

Section 45Z remains a major near-term earnings driver but creates a significant terminal-value issue.

For qualifying post-2025 fuel, the statutory amount is generally $0.20 per gallon or $1.00 per gallon if prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements are met, multiplied by the applicable emissions factor. The prior higher statutory amount specifically available to SAF does not continue after 2025. Current law applies the credit only through December 31, 2029.

Calumet’s recent disclosed tax-attribute estimates imply a rough effective value near $0.60 to $0.70 per gallon, subject to product mix, carbon intensity, transfer discounts, and timing. At 200 million gallons, that range would represent approximately $120 million to $140 million of annual gross tax attributes.

Timing is critical:

* The 200 million-gallon target is scheduled only for year-end 2028.
* Approximately 1 full year of target-level production would occur before current expiration.
* A 3-month delay in 2029 could reduce eligible target-rate production by approximately 50 million gallons.
* At $0.60 to $0.70 per gallon, that delay could reduce gross tax attributes by approximately $30 million to $35 million.
* A 6-month delay could reduce gross attributes by approximately $60 million to $70 million.

Section 45Z cash flows should be modeled as finite-duration cash flows through 2029 and not capitalized at a terminal EBITDA multiple unless an extension is enacted. Post-2029 project value must be supported by SAF premiums, RINs, state credits, yield improvement, operating efficiency, and physical-product margins.

RFS AND RINS

The 2026 and 2027 Renewable Fuel Standard volumes are supportive for domestic renewable diesel and SAF producers. Higher obligations support aggregate demand for advanced and biomass-based diesel RINs, but also stimulate competing capacity and feedstock demand.

RIN economics can be large relative to physical fuel margins but remain exposed to small-refinery exemptions, reallocation decisions, production growth, imports, RIN banking, and litigation.

MRL’s North American feedstock orientation could become more valuable if future regulations favor domestic production or regional feedstocks, but this should be treated as upside rather than a secured base-case assumption.

FEEDSTOCK ECONOMICS

The expansion increases annual feedstock consumption to approximately 2 billion pounds. Feedstock is likely to remain the largest variable cost and earnings sensitivity.

Illustrative annual gross feedstock cost equals:

* Approximately $800 million at $0.40 per pound.
* Approximately $1.2 billion at $0.60 per pound.
* Approximately $1.6 billion at $0.80 per pound.

Sensitivity is extreme:

* Every $0.01 per pound changes annual gross cost by approximately $20 million.
* Every $0.05 per pound changes annual gross cost by approximately $100 million.
* A $0.05 adverse move equals approximately 73 percent of the remaining project capital.
* A $0.01 per pound increase equals approximately $0.10 per target SAF gallon.

Feedstock purchasing performance can create or destroy more value in 1 year than modest construction-cost variance.

Waste feedstocks such as used cooking oil, tallow, and certain distillers corn oil streams can generate superior carbon-intensity economics but are scarce and command premiums. Virgin vegetable oils offer more supply but may produce less favorable lifecycle emissions and environmental-credit value.

Feedstock flexibility is valuable only if switching does not materially impair throughput, yield, catalyst life, hydrogen use, product quality, or tax-credit eligibility. The proper optimization metric is contribution margin after feedstock price, freight, pretreatment, RINs, Section 45Z, state credits, yield, hydrogen, catalyst use, and finished-product netback.

SAF OFFTAKE AND COMMERCIAL RISK

MRL has established commercial relationships that validate product quality and logistics, but disclosed volumes appear to cover only a minority of the 200 million-gallon target.

Contract quality is more important than announced volume. Relevant terms include firm versus optional quantities, take-or-pay protection, SAF premium formula, ownership of RINs and Section 45Z value, state-credit allocation, book-and-claim rights, carbon-intensity warranties, freight, blending, change-in-law treatment, counterparty credit, and duration.

SAF demand should grow through mandates and corporate decarbonization commitments, but the premium over renewable diesel is not guaranteed. The removal of the former higher statutory Section 45Z amount specifically for SAF increases dependence on airline willingness to pay, international mandates, state programs, and operating efficiency.

VALUATION FRAMEWORK

Project valuation should separate:

* Temporary Section 45Z and elevated policy cash flows.
* Recurring operating uplift.
* Future expansion and strategic option value.

Recurring uplift consists of higher throughput, SAF premium over renewable diesel, renewable LPG recovery, improved renewable naphtha yield, lower water usage, and reduced unit costs.

Every $0.10 per gallon of recurring contribution on 200 million SAF gallons equals approximately $20 million of annual EBITDA. At an illustrative 8 times EBITDA multiple, this equals approximately $160 million of gross enterprise value before debt, minority interests, cash sweeps, taxes, maintenance capital, and CMR opportunity cost.

Illustrative sustainable incremental EBITDA scenarios are:

* $50 million of EBITDA: approximately $400 million of gross value at 8 times, or approximately $263 million net of remaining capital before other adjustments.
* $75 million of EBITDA: approximately $600 million of gross value, or approximately $463 million net of remaining capital.
* $100 million of EBITDA: approximately $800 million of gross value, or approximately $663 million net of remaining capital.

These are sensitivities rather than forecasts. Value attributable to Calumet common equity will be lower after DOE debt, accrued interest, preferred minority claims, retained liquidity, cash sweeps, lease obligations, and CMR opportunity cost.

KEY RISKS

* Q4 2026 turnaround delay or cost overrun.
* Underperformance of reused CMR equipment.
* Lower-than-expected SAF yield.
* Hydrogen constraints or higher natural-gas cost.
* Feedstock inflation and scarcity.
* SAF premium compression.
* Lower RIN values.
* Section 45Z expiration after 2029.
* Insufficient contracted offtake.
* Higher logistics and blending costs.
* Excessive working-capital consumption.
* Delayed final DOE draw.
* Restricted cash distributions from MRL.
* Existing minority preference and strategic rights.
* Foregone CMR refining value.
* Unidentified lease, decommissioning, or refurbishment costs.
* Inability to stabilize production before March 2029 DOE servicing.

KEY CATALYSTS AND DILIGENCE ITEMS

* Filing and review of the executed amended DOE agreement.
* Receipt of the final $34 million DOE draw.
* Disclosure of the CMR lease.
* Successful Q4 2026 tie-in and restart.
* Achievement of more than 80 million gallons by year-end 2026.
* Achievement of more than 120 million gallons during 2027.
* Additional long-term SAF offtake.
* Disclosure of SAF yield, hydrogen use, unit cost, and netbacks.
* Reconciliation of total capital spent and excluded costs.
* Evidence that MRL can fund the remaining $103 million internally.
* Resolution or strategic monetization of the existing minority interest.
* Completion of fractionation and hydrogen projects in 2028.
* Achievement of 200 million gallons by year-end 2028.
* Stable operation before March 2029 debt servicing.
* Legislative action on Section 45Z before December 31, 2029.

OVERALL CONCLUSION

The revised MaxSAF plan is materially superior to the original Phase 2 proposal on capital efficiency, financing feasibility, dilution, and construction risk. Eliminating approximately $538 million of required 3rd-party equity and avoiding as much as $624 million of additional DOE debt materially improve downside protection and preserve strategic flexibility.

The project is not simply a 140 million-gallon incremental volume expansion. Much of the SAF increase will come from converting renewable diesel into SAF. Sustainable value therefore depends on the SAF-versus-renewable-diesel netback after hydrogen, yield, logistics, and policy effects.

The $137 million remaining capital figure supports potentially attractive paybacks but may exclude meaningful economic costs. Full underwriting requires reconciliation of prior spending, lease economics, foregone CMR earnings, working capital, refurbishment, decommissioning, and sustaining capital.

Near-term economics could be highly attractive because Section 45Z, RINs, SAF premiums, and higher-value product recovery may generate cash flows disproportionate to the remaining capital. However, only approximately 1 full year of target-level production is scheduled before the current Section 45Z expiration. Post-2029 economics must therefore be attractive without assuming a tax-credit extension.

The probability-weighted value of MRL has likely increased because the project is now substantially more financeable and less exposed to catastrophic megaproject failure. Confirmation of durable value requires successful Q4 integration, quantified SAF yield improvement, disciplined feedstock procurement, larger contracted offtake, transparent cash-flow reporting, and evidence that earnings remain robust after temporary policy support declines.

Across the gen AI infrastructure complex, implied volatility has compressed sharply over the past several weeks — with most names sitting at or near the bottom of their 1-year IV ranges — even as spot prices remain well below their peaks on a 3-month basis. This is a classic post-event vol crush environment: earnings and other binary catalysts have passed, realized vol has declined, and the market is no longer pricing in near-term uncertainty. The VIX at 15.84 confirms the broad market backdrop is complacent.
PERFORMANCE — 3-MONTH CUMULATIVE TOTAL RETURN
The cohort is broadly underperforming the SPX (+1.41% 3M) and is mixed vs. the NDX (-3.32% 3M). ANET is the clear standout; AVGO and SMCI are the laggards on a 3-month basis, though SMCI has staged a sharp 1-month recovery (+30.2%).
IMPLIED VOLATILITY — THE VOL DOWN PICTURE
The vol compression is most striking in the highest-quality, most liquid names. NVDA’s 30-day ATM IV sits at 32.2 — an IV rank of just 2 out of 100, meaning it has been cheaper only 2% of the time over the past year. CEG, GEV, and VST are all at rank 1. VIX: 15.84
KEY CATALYSTS BEHIND THE VOL CRUSH
•NVDA (Aug 27): 1M ATM IV dropped 7.43 ppts — a 4.4 z-score move — as shares rallied 7.5% to ~$225. $MPC $PBF $VLO $CVX CALIFORNIA CRUDE DISLOCATION AND REFINER RENT CAPTURE (1/x)

EXECUTIVE CONCLUSION

The Argus article identifies a genuine and economically significant dislocation in California’s petroleum market. The closure of Phillips 66’s 139,000 b/d Los Angeles refinery and Valero’s 145,000 b/d Benicia refinery removed approximately 284,000 b/d of crude-processing capacity, equivalent to approximately 17.5 percent of California’s pre-closure refining capacity. The same closures simultaneously reduced demand for California-produced crude and reduced the supply of locally manufactured gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. The result is an unusually favorable combination for the surviving refiners: greater bargaining power over geographically constrained crude producers and greater pricing leverage in an increasingly capacity-short finished-product market. The transfer of economic rent is therefore occurring in 2 directions at the same time, from California upstream producers through weaker crude realizations and from consumers through wider refining margins. 

The article’s central conclusion is directionally correct, but the mechanism is more nuanced than a simple increase in California crude availability. H1 2026 California crude receipts declined approximately 4.2 percent year over year, from approximately 56.6 million barrels to 54.2 million barrels. Foreign crude receipts declined much more sharply, by approximately 18.7 percent, from approximately 147.6 million barrels to 119.9 million barrels. Total refinery crude receipts fell approximately 12.2 percent. California crude therefore gained share primarily because surviving refiners displaced imported barrels with discounted local supply, not because aggregate California production had already increased materially on a year-over-year basis. California-origin crude represented approximately 25.3 percent of H1 2026 receipts, compared with approximately 23.2 percent in H1 2025, and reached approximately 28.4 percent in June 2026. The immediate investment conclusion is that import substitution, rather than absolute statewide production growth, is currently providing the principal feedstock benefit. 

The opportunity is most directly concentrated at the surviving Los Angeles refining assets. Marathon Petroleum’s 365,000 b/d Los Angeles refinery appears to offer the largest absolute earnings exposure because of its scale and the reported doubling of California crude runs during 2Q26. PBF Energy’s Torrance refinery offers the clearest disclosed incremental exposure, with management indicating an increase of approximately 25,000-30,000 b/d in onshore California crude processing. Valero’s 85,000 b/d Wilmington refinery is considerably smaller but is expected to process record California crude volumes. Chevron’s 269,000 b/d El Segundo refinery is also positioned to benefit, although the company has provided less specific disclosure regarding incremental local crude intake. These 4 major Los Angeles-area refineries represent approximately 879,000 b/d of capacity, or approximately 65.7 percent of current statewide refining capacity. 

The benefit should not be interpreted as a permanent or unlimited gross-margin windfall. Heavy California crude carries lower product yields, higher residual output, greater coking requirements, higher refinery fuel consumption, greater hydrogen demand, and potentially higher fouling, corrosion, catalyst, sulfur-removal, wastewater, and maintenance costs than lighter imported crude. The relevant economic measure is not the headline crude discount but the discount after adjustment for quality, yield, logistics, operational limits, and incremental processing expense. The surviving complex refineries can capture a meaningful portion of the discount because they possess the necessary conversion equipment, but their capacity to absorb incremental heavy crude is constrained by cokers, hydrocrackers, hydrotreaters, hydrogen systems, sulfur plants, metallurgy, and product-market demand.

The dislocation is likely to persist until at least 1 of 4 balancing mechanisms occurs: San Pablo Bay pipeline service is restored at economically meaningful volumes; California crude production declines; Los Angeles refiners materially increase local crude intake; or additional refining capacity is restarted or constructed. The 1st mechanism is the most credible medium-term release valve. California Resources Corporation’s proposed acquisition of Crimson Midstream, including the San Pablo Bay pipeline system, creates a potential route for restoring Central Valley crude access to Bay Area refineries. The transaction is strategically important because even a modest improvement in producer market access can create value materially greater than the standalone pipeline earnings. However, the pipeline’s recent zero nominations, elevated tariff, uncertain refinery demand, heating requirements, regulated economics, and potential rehabilitation needs make a rapid return to high utilization uncertain. 

The highest-conviction relative-value conclusion is favorable for surviving Los Angeles conversion capacity and unfavorable for unprotected California crude production. The cleanest physical-market expression is effectively long complex Los Angeles refining margins and short the California crude location and quality basis. Public-equity implementation is less straightforward because Marathon Petroleum is highly diversified, Chevron is vertically integrated, Valero faces Benicia closure costs and lost capacity, PBF carries substantial operational and financial volatility, and California Resources is attempting to internalize part of the midstream bottleneck. The dislocation is therefore more powerful as a refinery-level and commodity-basis thesis than as a simple directional equity call.

CORE MARKET MECHANISM

California has developed an unusual combination of a locally long crude market and a locally short refined-product market. Crude production remains concentrated in mature fields with limited transportation alternatives, while the state’s refinery system is contracting. Finished products must meet California-specific specifications, including CARBOB gasoline requirements, and the state has limited pipeline connectivity with the Gulf Coast refining system. Additional gasoline supply must therefore be sourced largely through long-distance waterborne imports from suitably configured refineries. EIA estimated that the Phillips 66 and Valero closures represented approximately 17 percent of California refining capacity and approximately 11 percent of total West Coast capacity. West Coast gasoline imports exceeded 210,000 b/d on a 4-week average basis in May 2025, illustrating the increasing role of imported products even before both closures had been fully reflected in the market balance. 

The refinery closures affect the crude and product markets in opposite directions. On the crude side, refinery demand curves shift inward. California producers must compete for fewer refinery bids, and the remaining refiners can demand larger discounts for quality, transportation, scheduling flexibility, and operational inconvenience. On the product side, local supply curves shift inward. Fewer refineries produce California-specification gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, increasing reliance on inventories and waterborne imports. The surviving refiners therefore purchase feedstock in a market where they possess increasing oligopsony power and sell products into a market where concentration and import dependence are rising.

This asymmetry is structurally more important than the absolute amount of crude being produced. California crude cannot freely access national or international markets. The barrels are often heavy, require specialized handling, and face a transportation network designed around specific intrastate refinery destinations. California gasoline, by contrast, is priced against the marginal cost of obtaining compliant replacement supply from distant sources. Local crude prices can therefore weaken even while local gasoline prices and refinery cracks strengthen. The same refinery can capture both the discounted feedstock and the elevated replacement-value product price.

The closure effect is not evenly distributed across all California crude. Crude previously consumed at Benicia does not automatically become available to Los Angeles refiners at zero incremental logistics cost. The idling of the San Pablo Bay pipeline has segmented the state into increasingly distinct northern and southern crude markets. Central Valley barrels capable of moving south can pressure Los Angeles crude differentials, while Bay Area refineries can rely more heavily on waterborne crude. Transportation access, crude quality, contractual obligations, pipeline nominations, heating capability, storage availability, and refinery compatibility determine the realized discount on each barrel.

VALIDATION FROM STATE CRUDE FLOWS

California refinery receipts provide strong evidence that the surviving refiners are substituting local crude for foreign supply. California-origin receipts averaged approximately 299,000 b/d during H1 2026, compared with approximately 313,000 b/d during H1 2025. Foreign receipts fell from approximately 815,000 b/d to approximately 662,000 b/d over the same period. Alaska receipts were approximately unchanged at 223,000 b/d. The decline in foreign crude accounted for approximately 92.8 percent of the total reduction in H1 refinery receipts, while the decline in California crude accounted for approximately 8.0 percent, subject to rounding and smaller classification effects. The surviving system therefore protected local crude intake disproportionately despite materially lower aggregate runs. 

The sequential monthly pattern is more supportive of the Argus thesis than the H1 year-over-year comparison alone. California crude receipts increased from approximately 262,000 b/d in December 2025 to approximately 269,000 b/d in January 2026, approximately 293,000 b/d in March, approximately 320,000 b/d in April, approximately 333,000 b/d in May, and approximately 332,000 b/d in June. The local share of total crude receipts increased from approximately 21.5 percent in December 2025 to approximately 28.4 percent in June 2026. The acceleration during 2Q26 is consistent with the reported increases at PBF, Marathon Petroleum, and Valero. 

The data also establish an important limitation. A rising share of refinery feed does not necessarily indicate rising upstream production or rising absolute refinery demand for California crude. The share can rise because foreign crude imports decline faster than local receipts. That distinction is material for valuation. Refiners can capture an import-substitution benefit without California upstream volumes increasing, while producers can still experience declining output and weaker price realizations simultaneously. The current market is therefore best characterized as a reallocation of refinery demand toward discounted local barrels within a shrinking aggregate crude-processing system.

The substitution process can continue only while local crude remains economically preferable to imported alternatives and while refinery conversion units can handle the changing slate. Once crude-unit, coker, sulfur, hydrogen, or product-yield constraints bind, additional local supply must clear through a wider discount, additional blending, storage accumulation, production curtailment, or restored pipeline access. The marginal value of incremental local crude is therefore nonlinear. Early substitution barrels can replace high-cost imports with limited operational disruption; later barrels require progressively greater discounts to compensate for quality degradation and refinery bottlenecks.

REFINING CAPACITY CONTRACTION AND MARKET CONCENTRATION

California’s current operable refinery capacity is approximately 1.338 million b/d, based on California Energy Commission data. The largest assets are Marathon Petroleum’s 365,000 b/d Los Angeles refinery, Chevron’s 269,000 b/d El Segundo refinery, Chevron’s approximately 245,000 b/d Richmond refinery, PBF’s 160,000 b/d Torrance refinery, PBF’s approximately 156,000 b/d Martinez refinery, and Valero’s 85,000 b/d Wilmington refinery. The Phillips 66 Los Angeles and Valero Benicia closures reduced capacity by approximately 284,000 b/d from an estimated pre-closure base of approximately 1.622 million b/d. 

Capacity concentration has risen materially. A simplified operator-level Herfindahl-Hirschman Index calculated from nameplate capacity increases from approximately 2,181 before the closures to approximately 2,832 after the closures. The calculation is not equivalent to a formal antitrust product-market analysis because refinery output slates, geographic reach, import competition, proprietary logistics, planned maintenance, and actual utilization differ across facilities. Nevertheless, the increase indicates a substantial reduction in the number and diversity of refinery bids for crude and refinery offers for finished products. The concentration effect is particularly pronounced in Southern California, where Marathon Petroleum, Chevron, PBF, and Valero control nearly all major conversion capacity. 

The loss of capacity creates greater outage convexity. A 50,000 b/d unplanned outage represents a larger percentage of remaining regional production than it did before the closures. Inventory buffers are limited, replacement gasoline requires long shipping lead times, and imported cargoes may not perfectly match timing, grade, terminal, or blending requirements. This increases the probability that relatively small operational disruptions produce disproportionate movements in gasoline cracks and wholesale prices. It also increases the value of reliability at the surviving plants.

The same outage convexity can work against crude suppliers. When a major Los Angeles refinery experiences an outage, the immediate loss of crude demand can widen local differentials and create storage or pipeline congestion. A refinery owner therefore benefits from industry-wide capacity scarcity but remains exposed to severe negative operating leverage when its own facility is unavailable. Equity outcomes depend heavily on which refinery is operating and which refinery is impaired. A generalized long-refiner thesis must therefore be conditioned on asset reliability, turnaround schedules, and working-capital capacity.

THE DOUBLE-LEVERAGE MARGIN EFFECT

California refiners are currently benefiting from a combination of stronger product cracks and weaker local crude acquisition costs. California Energy Commission disclosures show the statewide volume-weighted gross gasoline refining margin increasing from approximately $0.44/gal in December 2025 to $0.49/gal in January 2026, $0.77/gal in February, $1.02/gal in March, $1.24/gal in April, and $1.29/gal in May before declining to $0.92/gal in June. Aggregate statewide gross gasoline refining margin increased from approximately $429 million in January to approximately $1.207 billion in May and remained approximately $887 million in June. These figures are self-reported, are not independently verified by the state, and should not be interpreted as refinery EBITDA or net profit. Nevertheless, they confirm a substantial widening in the gross difference between wholesale gasoline value and crude acquisition cost. 

The gross-margin expansion cannot be attributed solely to discounted California crude. Product cracks have also been affected by refinery closures, outages, import economics, freight, geopolitical conditions, inventory levels, seasonal gasoline specifications, and broader petroleum-market volatility. The significance of the Argus article is not that local crude caused the entire margin expansion, but that local crude discounts provide an additional and increasingly durable source of margin beneath an already strong product environment.

The 2 margin components have different durations. Product cracks can compress rapidly when inventories rebuild, imports arrive, demand weakens, or refinery utilization recovers. The California crude location discount is likely to be more persistent because it reflects physical transportation constraints and a reduced number of refinery buyers. A refinery earnings model should therefore avoid capitalizing the entire current product crack but can assign greater persistence to a portion of the local feedstock advantage, subject to San Pablo Bay pipeline developments and production trends.

A $5/bbl improvement in crude acquisition cost corresponds to approximately $0.119/gal of crude input before adjusting for refinery yields, losses, processing costs, and the allocation of crude cost across gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, residual products, petroleum coke, and asphalt. This is meaningful but materially smaller than the approximately $0.92-$1.29/gal statewide gross gasoline refining margins reported during March-June 2026. Product scarcity remains the larger driver of California consumer economics, while the crude discount creates an additional transfer of value toward the refiner.

$CLMT INDIANAPOLIS, Sept. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Calumet, Inc. (NASDAQ: CLMT) ("Calumet," "we," "our" or "us") announced today a new flight plan for its MaxSAF® expansion at Montana Renewables, LLC ("Montana Renewables" or "MRL"), an unrestricted subsidiary of Calumet. By repurposing proven, installed refining equipment from the adjacent Calumet Montana Refining ("CMR") facility, Montana Renewables expects to reach approximately 200 million gallons of annual Sustainable Aviation Fuel ("SAF") production and 17,000 barrels per day of total product sales by year-end 2028. The total remaining project capital spend for this expansion is $137 million, compared to the $1.2 billion megaproject contemplated in the original loan issued by the U.S. Department of Energy ("DOE") through its Office of Energy Dominance Financing ("EDF").

Reflecting the dramatically lower capital requirement, Montana Renewables and EDF have amended the Loan Guarantee Agreement ("LGA") originally executed in January 2025. Phase 2 DOE funding is reduced from up to $658 million to a single, final draw of $34 million, with the balance of the expansion self-funded from MRL earnings. The original agreement required the project's full equity to be committed before Phase 2 construction. The amended structure requires no third-party equity, thereby eliminating dilution and preserving a simple capital structure for future strategic opportunities while accelerating the benefits of increased throughput, SAF, improved yields, and reduced unit costs.

The centerpiece of the revised plan is the redeployment of selected CMR assets — a hydrotreater, hydrogen plant, and naphtha splitter — to Montana Renewables under a long-term lease. The tied-in hydrotreater creates a proprietary dual reactor system that runs in a "polishing" service rather than the industry-standard "cracking" service, delivering competitively advantaged SAF yields while lowering by-product production and reducing yield loss. Several additional modular components, including a third renewable fuels reactor currently offsite, provide the ability to expand capacity beyond 200 million gallons over time. 

Rather than a single large construction project, the new expansion is structured as six small, controllable, quick-payback projects, each designed to increase returns and reduce construction risk. Following constraint removal completed at the Spring 2026 turnaround, Montana Renewables is currently producing at a run-rate of 60 million gallons of SAF per year; expects to exceed an 80 million gallon run-rate by year-end 2026; surpass 120 million gallons by Spring 2027; and reach approximately 200 million gallons by year-end 2028. The program also captures approximately 20 million gallons per year of renewable propane and butane — previously burned as fuel gas — as saleable product, improves renewable naphtha yields, and reduces unit operating costs through scale and lower water usage.

The reconfiguration represents the next evolution of more than a decade of modernization at the Great Falls site under Calumet's ownership. The turnaround to complete the tie-in is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026 — timing that allows CMR to capture approximately $50 million of EBITDA at currently elevated global refining margins before the transition. CMR will remain in service, continuing to produce high-quality retail asphalt, retaining all employees, and providing shared cost efficiencies across the full site.

"Our amended agreement with the DOE facilitates innovative technology and domestic energy security at a fraction of the original cost," said Todd Borgmann, CEO of Calumet. "EDF's willingness to right-size the LGA reflects its ongoing support for Montana's largest agricultural investment. We look forward to our continued collaboration with the DOE on the success of this project."

"We've worked hard to unleash the ingenuity of our engineering and operational teams, and they developed a project that captures approximately 70% of the originally expected benefit while spending only 15% of the originally expected Phase 2 capital," Borgmann continued. "The DOE has kept our nation's energy independence goals at the forefront while demonstrating tremendous flexibility in thoughtfully working with us to adjust the loan. MRL was honored to be the first project to receive the support of the current Administration, and we thank the entire DOE team for its continued commitment to this key component of America's energy infrastructure. With the DOE's support, Montana Renewables continues to strengthen its position as one of the world's largest SAF producers while supporting regional agriculture, the Montana business community, our employees, and our shareholders."

The expansion increases MRL's total feedstock consumption to approximately 2 billion pounds of ranch- and farm-originated feedstocks, converted into American-made renewable jet fuel, diesel, and gasoline annually, while continuing to grow Montana's wage and tax base with highly skilled technical employment in a rural community.

Amended Loan Guarantee Structure

The DOE loan remains structured in two tranches. The first tranche of $782 million was funded in February 2025 and used to recapitalize MRL, including an additional $150 million equity investment by Calumet with cash on hand. Under the amended agreement, the remaining loan availability is reduced to a single, final draw of $34 million — down significantly from the previous additional draw of up to $658 million, which MRL expects to receive shortly, subject to the satisfaction of certain commercial, technical, and legal conditions precedent.

During construction, retained earnings from MRL are expected to supplement DOE funds to maintain debt at less than 55% of eligible spending. The loan retains its 15-year tenor and an annual interest rate of the U.S. Treasury rate plus 3/8%, with servicing of principal and interest deferred until MaxSAF® is commissioned. The March 2029 first servicing date and December 2039 maturity remain unchanged. The amended LGA will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission ("SEC"), and investors should refer to the filed agreement for complete terms.

About Montana Renewables

Montana Renewables (MRL) is a leading renewable fuel company located in Great Falls, Montana. We produce Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), Renewable Diesel, Renewable Hydrogen, and Renewable Naphtha. As one of only three SAF producers running at commercial scale in North America, we meet the increasing demand for sustainable jet fuels. As a Great Falls business leader, MRL offers high-paying jobs and career opportunities while supporting the local economy and contributing to the community's overall well-being.  Pacific Northwest farm and ranch operations ultimately provide MRL with sustainable, renewable, low-carbon feedstocks and agricultural byproducts including tallow, distillers corn oil, canola oil, used cooking oil and camelina oil.  These are converted to renewable transportation fuels which have lower emissions compared to conventional fossil fuels.  MRL is an unrestricted subsidiary of Calumet, Inc.

About Calumet

Calumet, Inc. (NASDAQ: CLMT) manufactures, formulates, and markets a diversified slate of specialty branded products and renewable fuels to customers across a broad range of consumer-facing and industrial markets. Calumet is headquartered in Indianapolis, Indiana and operates twelve facilities throughout North America.
