D4 RIN & SMALL REFINERY EXEMPTION POLICY: STATUS AND OUTLOOK

REGULATORY FRAMEWORK

The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), established in 2005 under the Clean Air Act, is administered by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The program requires refiners and importers of gasoline and diesel (obligated parties) to blend biofuels into transportation fuels or purchase tradeable credits — Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) — to demonstrate compliance.

- D4 RINs represent biomass-based diesel (biodiesel and renewable diesel). Each gallon of qualifying fuel generates RINs based on an equivalence value (currently 1.7 RINs/gallon for renewable diesel, proposed to drop to 1.6 in future years).
- Obligated parties submit RINs equal to their Renewable Volume Obligation (RVO), set annually by the EPA, to demonstrate compliance.
- The EPA is required to publish annual volume standards by November 30 for the forthcoming year, though this deadline has frequently been missed in practice.

RFS SET 2 FINAL RULE (FINALIZED MARCH 27, 2026)

The EPA finalized its "Set 2" rule on March 27, 2026, establishing record-high renewable fuel volume obligations for 2026 and 2027.

Category: Total RIN Obligation
2025 (Pre-Set 2): ~22 billion
2026 (Final): 25.82 billion
2027 (Final): 25.98 billion

Category: Biomass-Based Diesel (D4) RINs
2025 (Pre-Set 2): ~5.3 billion
2026 (Final): 8.86 billion
2027 (Final): Higher

Category: BBD Volume (gallons)
2025 (Pre-Set 2): 3.35 billion gal
2026 (Final): 5.4 billion gal
2027 (Final): 5.7 billion gal

Category: Conventional Biofuel (D6)
2025 (Pre-Set 2): 15 billion gal
2026 (Final): 15 billion gal
2027 (Final): 15 billion gal

The BBD mandate represents a ~67% increase from 2025 — the largest mandate increase in the program's history.

The Set 2 rule also aims to advance U.S. energy independence by prioritizing biofuels made from domestically sourced feedstocks.

SMALL REFINERY EXEMPTIONS (SREs)

AUGUST 2025 SRE BACKLOG CLEARANCE

In August 2025, the EPA finalized decisions on 175 SRE petitions spanning compliance years 2016–2024, granting 63 full exemptions and 77 partial exemptions, while denying approximately 28 petitions.

Key company outcomes from the August 22, 2025 batch included:

- Calumet (CLMT): Granted exemptions, slashing its RIN liability by over 75%.
- Delek (DK): Received more than half of its SRE petitions for 2019–2024 granted, described as the biggest beneficiary.
- CVR Energy / Wynnewood: Granted waivers for 2017–2024, cutting RIN obligations by 300M+ credits.

In November 2025, the EPA issued additional decisions — granting full exemptions to two petitions, partial exemptions to 12, and denying two — covering HF Sinclair and Phillips 66 facilities, while denying Chevron's requests.

In August 2026, Delek received a full exemption, while HF Sinclair and United Refining received partial exemptions, with three HF Sinclair requests denied.

SRE METHODOLOGY AND LEGAL RISK

The EPA's updated framework for evaluating SRE petitions — including the return of previously retired RINs — may face legal challenges due to inconsistencies between 2025 grants and prior-year methodology.

Delek is pursuing litigation against the EPA's decision to refund expired RINs for 2022 and prior years. Any future returns of legacy vintage RINs are likely to follow this precedent.

Wynnewood Refining and Calumet Shreveport had separately filed suits challenging EPA denials for the 2023 compliance year; Calumet subsequently dropped its case after the EPA replaced its denial with a new administrative decision.

SRE REALLOCATION MECHANISM

A critical feature of the Set 2 final rule is the reallocation of 70% of renewable fuel volumes lost to SREs for compliance years 2023–2025 back to non-exempt obligated parties, effectively restoring approximately 2.03 billion gallons (~2 billion RINs) of previously lost demand.

The EPA is also expected to propose a rule for reallocating exempted volumes from 2023 and later compliance years, which would further increase RIN demand from non-exempt refiners.

CARRYFORWARD / RIN BANK PROVISIONS

- RINs are vintage-dated and generally valid for use in the compliance year generated or the following year. Expired RINs cannot be used for compliance — a key issue in the August 2025 SRE decisions, where a majority of refunded RINs had already expired, limiting practical relief.
- The RIN bank entered 2026 with an estimated carryover of approximately 2.9 billion RINs, but this buffer is diminishing rapidly given strong 2026–27 mandates and limited domestic biomass-based diesel capacity.
- The D4/D5 RIN bank is projected to be in a slight deficit of approximately 40 million RINs in 2026, with further tightening expected in 2027.
- D4 RIN generation through July 2026 was approximately 4.66 billion RINs, up ~17% year-over-year, outpacing overall RIN generation growth of ~8%.

COMPLIANCE YEAR OUTLOOK: 2025, 2026, AND 2027

2025 COMPLIANCE YEAR

- The EPA delayed the standard September 1, 2026 compliance deadline for 2025 RFS obligations and committed to issuing all pending 2025 SRE decisions by end of August 2026.
- Approximately 34 SRE petitions for 2025 remain pending as of late August 2026, with the EPA considering a compliance deadline extension of 30–90 days.
- The pending 2025 SRE decisions are estimated at approximately 1.8 billion RINs — significantly above the EPA's own projected 991 million reallocation baseline in the Set 2 rule.
- Up to 600 million 2025 RINs may be held by small refiners awaiting exemption decisions, creating near-term uncertainty in the compliance market.
- Some refiners (e.g., Wynnewood/CVR) continue to recognize 100% of their RIN obligation — approximately $77 million per quarter — pending resolution of their 2025 SRE petition.

2026 COMPLIANCE YEAR

- Record-high RVOs under Set 2 are in effect. D4 RIN prices exceeded $2/RIN in H1 2026 following the March final rule, and have risen over 125% from Q2 2025 levels, averaging nearly $14/barrel equivalent in Q2 2026.
- If the 2025 SRE approach continues into 2026, exemptions could rise to approximately 2.1 billion RINs annually, which would exceed the reallocation built into mandates and potentially loosen obligations.
- Extrapolated 2026 batch volumes suggest domestic production will still fall short of the revised mandate, increasing reliance on net imports.
- The half-RIN provision for imported fuels and foreign feedstocks was deferred to 2028 or later, meaning imported renewable fuels continue to generate full RIN value through 2027.

2027 COMPLIANCE YEAR

- The D4+D5 RIN mandate is projected at 9.9 billion RINs in 2027, against estimated generation of only ~5.1 billion RINs — implying a significant structural shortfall requiring imports or bank drawdown.
- The half-RIN provision for non-U.S. feedstocks is expected to be enforced starting in 2028, with the administration aiming to support domestic farmers.
- SRE methodology is assumed by some analysts to remain consistent through 2028, though legal challenges could alter the framework.

KEY MARKET IMPLICATIONS

- RIN prices are adding approximately $0.40/gallon to U.S. gasoline prices; RFS compliance costs exceed all other combined operating costs for many small refineries.
- D4 prices are expected to continue outperforming feedstock costs through 2027, despite near-term volatility tied to SRE issuance expectations.
- Soybean oil is expected to be the marginal feedstock, with the U.S. biofuel sector projected to consume 17.3 billion pounds of soybean oil in the 2026–2027 marketing year.
- Congressional efforts to legislate a compromise on SRE eligibility stalled in early 2026, with large and small refiners unable to reach consensus.

$VLO $MPC $PSX $DINO DILUENT EXECUTIVE ASSESSMENT (1/x)

Diluent is one of the highest-leverage constraints on Venezuelan oil production. It is not a minor blending additive. For a large portion of Orinoco Belt production, diluent is the material that converts an extra-heavy, highly viscous reservoir fluid into a crude blend that can be pumped through gathering systems, transported approximately 150-300 kilometers to the coast, stored in tanks, loaded onto tankers and processed by a refinery. A sustained interruption in diluent supply can force production cuts within days or weeks even when wells, reservoirs and export demand remain available.

Venezuela currently requires approximately 80-105kb/d of imported heavy naphtha and other light hydrocarbons. Heavy-naphtha imports were approximately 105kb/d in February 2026, 93kb/d in May and 81kb/d in July. PDVSA has historically described its normal requirement as approximately 100kb/d. Part of this volume is used for domestic gasoline production, but most of the strategically critical requirement is associated with blending extra-heavy Orinoco crude. 

At current market prices, this is a multi-billion-dollar annual supply chain. A broad international naphtha benchmark was approximately $746 per metric ton on August 28, 2026. Using a representative heavy-naphtha density range of 0.75-0.78 metric tons per cubic meter, that equates to approximately $89-$92/bbl before the U.S. Gulf Coast quality basis, terminal charges, freight, insurance, working-capital costs and demurrage. A reasonable screening estimate for delivered heavy naphtha into Venezuela is therefore approximately $92-$100/bbl under orderly conditions and potentially above $100-$110/bbl during a stressed market or extended port delays. At import volumes of 81-105kb/d, the annualized gross cash requirement is approximately $2.7bn-$3.8bn. 

The gross cash requirement is not the same as the ultimate economic cost. When naphtha is exported as part of Merey or diluted crude oil, the diluent is sold to the crude buyer as part of the blended barrel. Venezuela recovers some of the naphtha’s value through the higher export volume. The true economic burden is the difference between the price paid for the light diluent and the lower price received for that same molecule when it is embedded in a discounted heavy crude, plus freight, financing, handling, evaporation, contamination and operating costs. Where the diluent is separated at a functioning upgrader and returned to the field, it behaves more like working inventory and only losses and make-up volumes must be replaced.

The U.S. Gulf Coast can supply Venezuela’s current requirement in aggregate, but a large Venezuelan production expansion would materially tighten the specialized diluent market. PADD 3 natural-gas plants produced approximately 562kb/d of natural gasoline and 109kb/d of condensate and scrubber oil in May 2026, or approximately 671kb/d combined. Current Venezuelan imports of 81-105kb/d are equivalent to approximately 12%-16% of that broad liquids pool. However, most of that pool is not automatically suitable for Venezuelan extra-heavy crude, and refinery-produced heavy naphtha is chemically different from highly paraffinic natural gasoline or condensate. The relevant constraint is therefore not aggregate U.S. light-hydrocarbon availability. It is the availability of correctly specified, asphaltene-compatible, heavy or full-range naphtha at a competitive price. 

An additional 500kb/d of raw Orinoco extra-heavy production could require approximately 125-214kb/d of incremental diluent if the diluent represents 20%-30% of the final export blend. At an assumed delivered price of $95/bbl, that would require approximately $4.3bn-$7.4bn of gross annual diluent purchases. The upper end would be equivalent to approximately 32% of current PADD 3 natural-gasoline and condensate production before considering competing gasoline, petrochemical, export and Canadian heavy-oil demand. A 500kb/d Venezuelan production ramp is therefore not merely an upstream drilling program. It would require a dedicated, contractually secured diluent system containing supply agreements, storage, tanker capacity, field pipelines, blending facilities, quality controls and substantial working capital.

WHAT DILUENT IS

OFAC defines diluent as a light hydrocarbon liquid, including natural-gas condensate, naphtha or light crude, that is added to heavy crude or bitumen to reduce viscosity and density so the resulting blend can be transported, exported, stored or processed more easily. This definition captures the 3 principal diluent families used in Venezuela. 

The Orinoco Belt produces crude that can be approximately 8°-14° API before blending. At reservoir and ambient temperatures, some of this oil has a consistency closer to bitumen than to conventional crude. Artificial-lift systems can bring it to the surface, but the undiluted material creates excessive pressure drop in gathering systems and export pipelines. Pumping rates fall, pump energy rises, pipeline restart risk increases and storage-tank handling becomes difficult. Dilution lowers both density and, more importantly, viscosity.

Density and viscosity must be distinguished. API gravity is useful for custody transfer and broad blend design, but pipeline operability is principally a viscosity and pressure-drop problem. A relatively small change in diluent concentration can produce a disproportionately large change in viscosity. A blend that meets a nominal 16° API target can still be unstable or operationally unacceptable if its asphaltenes precipitate, its viscosity remains above pipeline specifications, its pour point is too high or its sediment content becomes excessive.

The preferred Venezuelan product is commonly described as heavy, full-range or N+A naphtha. “Heavy” refers to the heavier portion of the naphtha boiling range, not to heavy crude. EIA defines naphtha broadly as a refined or partially refined petroleum fraction boiling at approximately 122°F-400°F. N+A refers to naphthenes plus aromatics, chemical families that generally provide stronger solvency for asphaltene-rich crude than highly paraffinic natural gasoline. 

The distinction is economically important. A very light condensate may achieve a target API gravity using fewer barrels, but a highly paraffinic condensate can destabilize asphaltenes and create sludge, tank bottoms, plugged filters, fouled heat exchangers and inconsistent cargo quality. A somewhat heavier naphtha may require more volume but provide a more stable blend. The economically optimal diluent is therefore not necessarily the product with the highest API gravity or lowest headline price. It is the product that delivers the lowest total cost per barrel of transportable, stable and refinery-acceptable blended crude.

HOW DILUENT IS PRODUCED

REFINERY-PRODUCED NAPHTHA

Heavy naphtha is primarily produced during crude-oil refining. Crude first enters an atmospheric distillation unit, where it is separated by boiling range into gases, naphtha, kerosene, distillate, gas oil and atmospheric resid. The naphtha stream is usually stabilized and split into light and heavy fractions. Light naphtha is generally directed toward isomerization, gasoline blending, solvents or petrochemical use. Heavy naphtha is normally hydrotreated and sent to a catalytic reformer.

Catalytic reforming converts relatively low-octane naphtha into high-octane reformate used in the gasoline pool and produces hydrogen as a valuable byproduct. Exporting heavy naphtha to Venezuela therefore has an opportunity cost for the supplying refinery. The refinery may lose reformer throughput, high-octane reformate production, aromatics production and some hydrogen output unless it has surplus naphtha or can replace the feed from another source. 

The quantity and quality of naphtha produced by a refinery depend on the refinery’s crude slate. Light crude generally yields more naphtha and light distillates than heavy crude. The U.S. Gulf Coast’s substantial Permian and Eagle Ford crude intake creates a deep potential naphtha pool. Refiners can also aggregate straight-run naphtha from multiple crude units and process streams, although diluent suppliers must carefully control sulfur, olefins, vapor pressure, distillation range and blend compatibility.

Heavy virgin naphtha is usually more suitable than cracked naphtha. Catalytically cracked and coker naphthas can contain higher olefins, sulfur, nitrogen and instability precursors. They may require hydrotreating before use and can create additional quality risk. Venezuelan buyers generally prefer a consistent straight-run, heavy or full-range N+A specification rather than an opportunistic mixture of refinery streams.

NATURAL-GAS CONDENSATE

Lease condensate is recovered from natural gas at field separators or stabilization facilities. It consists mainly of pentanes and heavier hydrocarbons that were in the gas phase under reservoir conditions but become liquid as pressure and temperature fall. The condensate may be stabilized to remove very light components and then sold directly, blended into crude or processed through a condensate splitter. 

A condensate splitter performs a simplified distillation process and separates condensate into LPG, light naphtha, heavy naphtha, kerosene-range material and heavier bottoms. The heavy-naphtha cut can be sold as reformer feed, petrochemical feedstock or diluent.

Condensate has the advantage of very high API gravity, often allowing a lower volumetric blending ratio than light crude or heavier naphtha. Its disadvantages can include high vapor pressure, substantial light-end losses, fire and vapor-management requirements, and potentially weak asphaltene solvency. The quality varies substantially by basin and gas stream. A condensate from a rich associated-gas field is not interchangeable with another field’s condensate without laboratory compatibility testing.

NATURAL GASOLINE AND PENTANES PLUS

Natural gasoline, also called pentanes plus, is produced at natural-gas-processing and NGL-fractionation facilities. Wet natural gas is processed to remove NGLs, which are then separated into ethane, propane, normal butane, isobutane and natural gasoline. EIA defines pentanes plus as a mixture consisting mostly of pentanes and heavier hydrocarbons extracted from natural gas and treats it as equivalent to natural gasoline. 

Natural gasoline is widely used as Canadian oil-sands diluent and could theoretically supply Venezuela. It benefits from high API gravity and deep U.S. Gulf Coast production. However, natural gasoline is generally more paraffinic and more volatile than the heavy N+A naphtha currently preferred for Venezuela. It can be blended with heavier aromatic material to improve solvency, but this adds another procurement and quality-control step.

LIGHT CRUDE OIL

Conventional light crude can also be used directly. It requires no refinery processing and generally presents lower vapor-pressure and asphaltene-instability risk than natural gasoline. Venezuela historically used domestic light and medium crudes, including production from eastern Venezuela, to produce export blends such as Merey.

Light crude’s disadvantage is its lower dilution efficiency. A 30°-40° API crude requires materially more barrels to reach the same final blend density than a 50°-70° API naphtha or condensate. Light crude is also a valuable refinery feedstock in its own right. Using it as diluent can divert supply from Venezuela’s domestic refineries or require expensive imports.

Venezuela resumed regular imports of light crude in 2025 because domestic medium- and light-crude production had declined. The decline was partly associated with insufficient gas reinjection and damaged gas-processing infrastructure in eastern Venezuela. Iran had supplied crude and condensate through a 2021-2023 exchange arrangement, but those flows subsequently declined amid payment and project disputes. 

RECYCLED UPGRADER NAPHTHA

The most capital-efficient long-term configuration is a closed diluent loop. Extra-heavy crude is diluted at the field, moved by pipeline to a coastal upgrader, and then distilled or flashed so the naphtha can be separated and returned to the field through a dedicated diluent pipeline. The remaining heavy stream is upgraded through coking, hydroprocessing or other conversion processes into synthetic crude.

The original Orinoco projects were designed around this model. One major pipeline system was designed for naphtha to constitute approximately 18%-20% of the transported blend, with a 510kb/d diluted-crude line and a 125kb/d diluent-return line. Other Orinoco projects used somewhat higher ratios. Technical studies describe diluent separation at the coastal upgrader and return to the production area as a means of reducing exposure to external diluent availability and price. 

The closed-loop system has a large upfront working-capital requirement because the pipeline, tanks and process units must initially be filled with diluent. Thereafter, imports are required primarily for operating losses, contamination, inventory expansion and outages. The system’s weakness is dependence on upgrader and return-pipeline reliability. If the upgrader is unavailable, raw extra-heavy crude may need to be exported as diluted crude, converting a largely recyclable inventory into a continuously consumed import requirement.

DILUENT TYPES AND RELATIVE ECONOMICS

Heavy N+A naphtha is generally the preferred material for current Venezuelan diluted-crude production. It combines strong viscosity reduction with better asphaltene solvency, manageable vapor pressure, refinery compatibility and an established U.S. Gulf Coast supply chain. Its principal disadvantage is price because it competes directly with catalytic reformers and petrochemical users.

Condensate and natural gasoline can reduce the required volume because of their higher API gravity. They may be attractive when Gulf Coast gas-processing output is abundant and reformer margins are high. Their limitations include high vapor pressure, evaporative loss, tank and ship vapor-management requirements and greater risk of precipitating asphaltenes. A condensate that performs well as Canadian dilbit diluent may not be suitable for a specific Venezuelan extra-heavy crude.

Light crude is operationally robust and can improve the overall refinery yield of the resulting blend. However, it requires a larger volume and can be more valuable in a refinery than as a diluent. Importing 1 barrel of 35° API crude may provide less density reduction than approximately 0.5 barrel of a much lighter condensate, depending on the target specification.

The correct optimization metric is the delivered cost per barrel of stable, transportable heavy crude, not the posted price per barrel of diluent. That calculation must include the required blend ratio, viscosity reduction, asphaltene stability, vapor losses, tank requirements, pipeline pressure, cargo quality, final crude yield and the price the refinery will pay for the resulting blend.

BLEND RATIOS AND MATERIAL BALANCE

Historical Orinoco project designs illustrate the range of possible ratios. Some designs contemplated approximately 18%-20% diluent in the final transported blend. Another project used 70kb/d of diluent within a 220kb/d transportation stream, equivalent to approximately 32%. Broader technical literature on extra-heavy oil and bitumen reports dilution ratios of approximately 24%-50%, depending on fluid properties, temperature, pipeline specifications and diluent quality. 

The distinction between “% of final blend” and “barrels of diluent per barrel of raw heavy” is important. A blend containing 20% diluent consists of 0.20 barrel of diluent and 0.80 barrel of raw heavy per 1 barrel of final product. The ratio is therefore 0.25 barrel of diluent per barrel of raw heavy. At 25% of the final blend, the ratio is 0.333 barrel per barrel of heavy. At 30%, the ratio is 0.429 barrel per barrel of heavy.

A simplified density calculation illustrates the effect of diluent quality. An 8° API extra-heavy crude blended to 16° API with 55° API naphtha would require approximately 21.5% diluent in the final blend, or approximately 0.274 barrel of diluent per barrel of raw heavy. Using 70° API condensate would reduce the density-based requirement to approximately 17.6%, or 0.214 barrel per barrel of raw heavy. Using 35° API light crude would require approximately 33.4% of the final blend, or approximately 0.50 barrel per barrel of raw heavy.

These calculations use only a volume-weighted density approximation. Actual blending decisions are normally governed by viscosity, vapor pressure, asphaltene stability, temperature, pipeline hydraulics and final cargo specifications. A high-API condensate that appears superior under a density calculation may be inferior if it destabilizes the crude.

The gross-barrel effect is economically significant. Producing 400kb/d of raw extra-heavy crude and blending it with 100kb/d of diluent generates 500kb/d of exportable diluted crude. Venezuela has historically used approximately 100kb/d of naphtha to dilute up to approximately 400kb/d of extra-heavy oil, broadly consistent with a 20% diluent share of the final blend. 

This means gross Venezuelan export statistics can overstate indigenous Venezuelan hydrocarbon production. If 1mb/d of diluted crude contains 20% imported naphtha, only 800kb/d is Venezuelan reservoir production and 200kb/d is imported light hydrocarbon returning to the world market inside the crude blend. The exact adjustment cannot be derived from national import figures because some imported naphtha is used for gasoline production, some Venezuelan exports are conventional crudes, and some upgraded crude has had the diluent removed and recycled.

VENEZUELA’S DOMESTIC DILUENT CAPABILITY

Venezuela possesses 3 potential domestic sources: light and medium crude production, refinery-produced naphtha and recycled upgrader naphtha. All 3 have deteriorated.

Domestic light- and medium-crude production has declined because many conventional eastern and western fields are mature, gas reinjection is inadequate, artificial-lift equipment is unreliable and field infrastructure has deteriorated. The national production mix has therefore shifted toward extra-heavy Orinoco barrels at the same time that the light hydrocarbons needed to move those barrels have become scarcer. 

Venezuela’s 6 principal refineries can produce naphtha, but the refining network has operated far below capacity. In April 2026 the system processed approximately 399kb/d, or only 31% of its nominal 1.29mb/d capacity. Crude units, catalytic crackers, reformers and supporting utilities have experienced repeated outages and power interruptions. Imported naphtha has consequently been used both for upstream dilution and to supplement domestic fuel production. 

Even a recovered refinery system would not automatically create a large surplus of diluent. Refinery naphtha is normally needed to feed catalytic reformers and produce domestic gasoline. Diverting it to Orinoco blending can reduce gasoline and reformate production. Venezuela therefore faces an internal allocation decision between using naphtha to produce exportable crude and using the same material to produce domestic motor fuel.

The legacy Orinoco upgraders provide the strongest theoretical domestic solution because they can recycle naphtha. However, the process depends on reliable distillation, coking, hydrotreating, hydrogen, utilities, power and return-pipeline operations. Upgrader outages increase external diluent demand at exactly the time that export revenues may be under pressure.

The most efficient national strategy would be to restore the existing closed-loop systems before constructing entirely new infrastructure. Every barrel of naphtha successfully recovered and returned can support repeated heavy-crude movements rather than requiring a new imported barrel for each export cycle.

$VLO $MPC $PSX $DINO EXECUTIVE ANSWER

Venezuela is capable of extracting oil without U.S. operators. It is already producing approximately 1.25mb/d, has operated one of the world’s largest petroleum industries for more than a century, retains a substantial domestic technical workforce, and possesses existing wells, gathering systems, blending facilities, upgraders, pipelines and export terminals. Venezuela also previously produced approximately 3.4-3.5mb/d. The country therefore does not lack the fundamental geological knowledge or basic operating capability required to produce oil. 

The more important conclusion is that Venezuela probably cannot convert the announced 65bn barrels into large, reliable and commercially competitive production on an acceptable timetable using PDVSA’s financial resources and operating organization alone. PDVSA can maintain existing production, reactivate selected wells and deliver modest brownfield growth. It is unlikely to rebuild the entire production, power, gas, pipeline, upgrading, port, data and service-company ecosystem required to return national output toward 2-3mb/d without substantial foreign capital, technology, equipment and operational assistance.

That foreign assistance does not technically have to come from the U.S. European, Chinese, Russian, Middle Eastern and other international companies possess many of the required capabilities. However, under the current commercial and geopolitical structure, U.S. participation is close to indispensable for a rapid, large-scale recovery because the U.S. controls the sanctions framework, provides the most convenient source of diluent, contains the natural refining market for Venezuela’s heavy crude, hosts several of the leading oilfield-service companies, and can provide access to dollar payments, shipping, marine insurance and international capital. OFAC’s current licenses specifically authorize U.S. goods, technology, software and services for Venezuelan oil and gas exploration, development and production, as well as repairs to oil, gas and electricity infrastructure. 

The distinction is therefore straightforward. Venezuela does not require the U.S. to physically operate every well. Venezuela does require a functioning external industrial and financial ecosystem to increase production materially. The U.S. is not the only possible provider of that ecosystem, but it is currently the most efficient and commercially important provider.

EXTRACTION IS ONLY 1 PART OF THE PROBLEM

The phrase “extracting the oil” understates the actual challenge. The complete commercial process contains at least 7 stages: reservoir characterization, drilling and well completion, artificial lift and pressure maintenance, field gathering, dilution or upgrading, pipeline transportation, and export loading. Venezuela can perform portions of this chain domestically. The weakness is the reliability and integration of the entire chain.

A producing well has limited economic value if there is insufficient electricity to operate pumps, insufficient natural gas for pressure support, no diluent to move the crude, a damaged pipeline between the field and terminal, inadequate storage, or a 30-day vessel queue at the export port. Venezuela’s principal constraint is consequently not simply subsurface extraction. It is the condition of the industrial system between the reservoir and the customer.

The current export system illustrates the problem. Venezuelan production has recovered to approximately 1.25mb/d, but exports have encountered a ceiling near that level as aging terminals, power outages, crude-quality problems and congestion have forced some vessels to wait as long as 30 days. Producing additional oil before increasing storage and terminal reliability would eventually fill tanks and force fields to reduce output. That occurred in early 2026 when export restrictions, insufficient storage and a shortage of diluent caused PDVSA to order production reductions at several joint ventures. 

CAPABILITY IN THE ORINOCO BELT

The Orinoco Belt contains most of Venezuela’s enormous reserve base. Its crude is generally extra-heavy, frequently near or below 10° API before blending, with high viscosity, sulfur, metals, asphaltenes and carbon residue. The reservoirs themselves are not uniformly difficult in the manner of ultra-deepwater or high-pressure offshore fields. Many Orinoco reservoirs can be developed using horizontal wells, progressive-cavity pumps or electric submersible pumps. The basic drilling and lifting technology is mature and has been used in Venezuela for decades.

The more difficult issue begins after the oil reaches the surface. Untreated Orinoco crude is generally too viscous for normal pipeline and marine transportation. It must either be mixed with lighter hydrocarbons or processed through an upgrader. Historical Orinoco systems have used diluent representing approximately 18%-25% of the transported blend, although the precise ratio varies by crude quality, temperature, pipeline specification and diluent type. The resulting diluted crude can be marketed as a grade such as Merey 16. 

This requirement creates a circular constraint. Venezuela’s legacy light- and medium-crude production has declined, leaving insufficient domestic light oil to dilute all prospective Orinoco output. Venezuela must therefore import naphtha, condensate or light crude before it can export a meaningful portion of its extra-heavy production. More than 100kb/d of U.S. naphtha was reportedly being shipped to Venezuela by August 2026 to support production and blending. Venezuela itself has acknowledged that further development of its heavy grades requires additional diluent. 

The alternative is upgrading. An upgrader uses coking, hydroprocessing and related processes to convert extra-heavy crude into a lighter synthetic crude. Venezuela built several major Orinoco upgraders during earlier joint-venture developments, including facilities associated with Petropiar, Petrocedeño and Petromonagas. These plants are expensive, mechanically complex, hydrogen-intensive and maintenance-intensive. Years of underinvestment and equipment deterioration have reduced reliability across the system.

Petropiar demonstrates both Venezuela’s capability and its dependence on foreign involvement. The integrated project produces extra-heavy oil, transports it to the coast and upgrades it. Chevron has a 30% interest, while PDVSA holds the majority. In early 2026, Petropiar was producing approximately 90kb/d of upgraded Hamaca crude and approximately 20kb/d of vacuum gas oil. Venezuela can operate this kind of asset, but its most reliable large project is operated through a long-standing partnership with a U.S. major rather than by PDVSA on a fully standalone basis. 

New greenfield Orinoco developments are substantially more difficult than restoring existing wells. A full project can require hundreds of wells, gathering stations, field treatment, diluent pipelines, storage, power generation, water systems, roads, worker accommodation, export pipelines and either an upgrader or long-term diluent supply. A field may contain billions of barrels but still require several billion dollars and 4-7 years before reaching material plateau production.

Venezuela could drill and operate portions of such developments itself. It cannot realistically finance and execute several large integrated projects simultaneously using current PDVSA cash flow, balance-sheet capacity and contractor relationships.

CAPABILITY IN LAKE MARACAIBO

Lake Maracaibo presents a different challenge. Much of the region contains conventional heavy, medium and light oil rather than the same extra-heavy resource found in the Orinoco Belt. Some Maracaibo crude can be transported and exported without the same degree of dilution or upgrading. This makes selected Maracaibo projects potentially faster and less expensive sources of incremental production.

However, the fields are mature and the infrastructure is exceptionally old. Production frequently requires well workovers, replacement pumps, gas lift, water injection, gas compression and pressure maintenance. Subsurface declines can be high, meaning gross additions are partly consumed by offsetting decline from the existing base.

The lake contains approximately 20,000 kilometers of pipelines and related infrastructure, much of it old, corroded, poorly mapped or inadequately maintained. A recently imported drilling rig struck a submerged oil pipeline while being transported through the lake, causing a leak that continued for months. The incident illustrates how even a relatively straightforward drilling program can be delayed by degraded midstream infrastructure. 

A foreign operator proposed spending approximately $1bn to raise production from 16kb/d to 60kb/d by refurbishing as many as 875 inactive wells before beginning new drilling. The project encountered insufficient gas for reservoir pressure, missing technical data and inadequate transportation for workers. These problems are not sophisticated reservoir challenges. They are symptoms of a degraded operating system. 

Maracaibo nevertheless provides the most plausible source of relatively rapid brownfield additions. Restoring shut-in wells, repairing gas compression, replacing artificial-lift equipment and increasing field reliability can produce barrels more quickly than constructing new Orinoco upgraders. The initial increase may be meaningful, but sustained growth requires continuous drilling and rehabilitation because the fields are mature.

WHAT PDVSA CAN DO WITHOUT U.S. OPERATORS

PDVSA can continue operating a substantial portion of existing production. Venezuela has engineers, geologists, drilling personnel, production operators, mechanics, terminal workers and refinery personnel. It retains detailed institutional knowledge of its principal basins and has operated fields through severe financial, political and sanctions constraints.

PDVSA can undertake relatively low-complexity activities such as restarting shut-in wells, replacing pumps, repairing flowlines, performing basic workovers, optimizing artificial lift, adjusting field blends and restoring individual compressors or gathering stations. These measures could stabilize production and create some incremental output.

Existing production near 1.25mb/d proves that Venezuela is not operationally incapable. However, this current production level is not fully indigenous in an economic or supply-chain sense. It is supported by imported diluent, foreign joint-venture partners, U.S. sanctions licenses, global trading companies, marine service providers and international buyers. Chevron’s Venezuelan ventures were producing approximately 240kb/d near the beginning of 2026, close to their then-current capacity, while U.S. naphtha imports have become an important input into Orinoco production. 

Without further U.S. participation, but with access to non-U.S. equipment, diluent and export markets, Venezuela could probably maintain production around current levels and deliver modest gains. It could source equipment and services from European, Asian, Middle Eastern and domestic suppliers. It could source diluent from Russia, Iran, Europe or other crude-producing countries. China and Russia have previously invested in Venezuelan projects, and European companies continue to maintain positions.

The difficulty would be cost, reliability and financing. Non-U.S. supply chains are often longer, financing is less available, payment structures are more cumbersome and access to U.S. Gulf Coast refiners is commercially valuable. Past payment defaults have also made service companies and contractors unwilling to extend ordinary trade credit. Eni alone reported billions of dollars of Venezuelan receivables, demonstrating that foreign participation does not automatically resolve payment risk. 

WHAT VENEZUELA CANNOT EASILY DO ALONE

Venezuela cannot efficiently rebuild reservoir databases, drill thousands of wells, restore gas infrastructure, rehabilitate the power grid, repair tens of thousands of kilometers of pipelines, rebuild upgraders, expand storage, restore export terminals and maintain domestic refining at the same time using current PDVSA resources.

The condition of PDVSA’s technical data is a significant constraint. Venezuela has not published a complete annual oil statistical bulletin since 2015. A recent cyberattack damaged systems, some geological and production data were lost, and portions must reportedly be reconstructed from paper records. SLB has been contracted to consolidate, digitize and modernize PDVSA’s reservoir and production databases. This is important because reliable field models, well histories, pressure data, production tests and facility records are prerequisites for determining where capital should be deployed. 

The power system is another binding constraint. Less than 40% of Venezuela’s electricity-generation capacity was reportedly available in May 2026, producing frequent outages. Oilfields require electricity for pumps, compressors, water injection, gathering systems, control systems and terminals. A field-development program cannot be separated from power restoration. 

Natural gas is also critical. PDVSA has reported a national gas deficit of approximately 500mmcf/d. Gas is needed for pressure maintenance, gas lift, steam generation, hydrogen production, power generation and refinery operations. Increasing oil production without restoring associated-gas collection and non-associated gas supply would intensify this bottleneck. 

Human capital cannot be restored immediately. Venezuela retains many capable employees, but substantial numbers of experienced engineers, geoscientists, project managers, refinery personnel and oilfield specialists left the country during the industry’s decline. Approximately 25,000 PDVSA employees reportedly departed during 2017 and January 2018 alone. Many Venezuelan professionals subsequently became important contributors to the Canadian oil-sands industry and other international petroleum sectors. A rapid Venezuelan recovery would require a combination of domestic training, returning expatriates and international personnel. 

WHY U.S. ASSISTANCE IS PARTICULARLY VALUABLE

The most valuable U.S. contribution is not federal ownership of drilling rigs. It is the combination of private operating capability and government-enabled commercial access.

Chevron provides the most immediate operating platform. It has long-standing interests in Petropiar, Petroboscán and other Venezuelan ventures, existing personnel, field knowledge, production infrastructure and established export channels. Chevron’s projects were producing approximately 240kb/d near the beginning of 2026, demonstrating that the company already operates at a scale large enough to affect national output. Its proposed restructuring and expansion around Petropiar and adjacent Orinoco acreage could deliver production more rapidly than a new entrant beginning without data, staff or infrastructure. 

U.S.-based oilfield-service companies can provide reservoir evaluation, directional drilling, completions, artificial lift, pressure pumping, well testing, production optimization, digital systems and integrated project management. SLB’s current data contract is an early example. Halliburton, Baker Hughes and Weatherford possess other relevant technologies and extensive historical experience in Venezuela.

The U.S. Gulf Coast is the most logical source of naphtha and other diluents. The sailing distance is short, Gulf Coast refiners and petrochemical plants produce suitable blendstocks, and a natural 2-way trade can be established: diluent moves south and Venezuelan heavy crude moves north. OFAC General License 47B explicitly authorizes sales of U.S.-origin diluent to Venezuela under the current framework. 

The U.S. also provides the most natural demand center. Gulf Coast refineries have extensive coking, hydrocracking, sulfur recovery and hydrogen capacity and were historically configured to process Venezuelan heavy-sour crude. Reliable U.S. offtake improves project financing because lenders and operators can underwrite a known destination and pricing mechanism.

The regulatory contribution is equally important. U.S. licenses now authorize oilfield goods and services, diluent exports, petroleum purchases, transport, insurance, refinery processing and specified company operations. Without a durable sanctions and licensing framework, even technically capable non-U.S. companies would remain exposed to secondary sanctions, dollar-clearing limitations, vessel restrictions and insurance problems. 

HOW MUCH CAN VENEZUELA ADD WITHOUT A FULL REBUILD

The first increments do not require rebuilding the entire industry. Near-term production can be increased by drawing down inventories, restoring shut-in wells, increasing diluent supply, repairing pumps, reactivating gas compression, improving power availability and increasing workover activity. This represents the low-hanging-fruit phase.

A reasonable range for sustainable incremental production from these measures is approximately 100-300kb/d over 1-2 years. A more aggressive outcome approaching 500kb/d is technically possible if many existing wells and projects are below physical capacity, but such an increase would require simultaneous improvement in diluent, storage, pipelines and terminals. Industry executives have suggested that as much as 500kb/d could potentially be added rapidly, while other forecasts place Venezuela at approximately 1.3-1.4mb/d within 2 years. The lower range should be considered more defensible until export and infrastructure constraints are visibly resolved. 

The current approximately 1.25mb/d production level is already near the upper end of what the present export and blending system appears capable of handling reliably. Venezuela’s own 2026 target was approximately 1.37mb/d by year-end. Reaching that level is plausible without an entirely new industrial architecture, but it still requires imported diluent and external market access. 

Moving toward 1.5-1.8mb/d is materially more difficult. It would require sustained drilling, larger workover programs, additional artificial-lift equipment, field gas restoration, higher diluent imports, storage rehabilitation and meaningful improvements at José and other terminals. Several billion dollars of annual investment would probably be required.

Moving beyond approximately 2mb/d would require major project development rather than maintenance-led recovery. New Orinoco well pads, gathering systems, power, pipelines and either additional upgrading or a permanently larger diluent supply would be necessary. Mature conventional fields would also require continuous drilling and secondary-recovery investment to offset decline.

COST OF RECOVERY

PDVSA estimated in 2021 that approximately $58bn would be required to return crude production to the 1998 level of approximately 3.4mb/d. It separately identified approximately $7.65bn for pipelines, gas injection, terminals and refining infrastructure. That estimate predates several additional years of deterioration and should be viewed as a lower-bound historical reference rather than a current fixed budget. 

An independent 2026 analysis estimated that Venezuela could reach approximately 2mb/d by 2032 and 3mb/d by 2040 if investment averaged roughly $8bn-$9bn annually, in addition to capital required to hold existing output flat. The estimated cumulative investment above 1.4mb/d was approximately $41bn to reach 2mb/d and another approximately $75bn to move from 2mb/d toward 3mb/d. These figures are scenario estimates, but they demonstrate that the announced approximately $100bn private-investment ambition is broadly consistent with the scale of a national recovery rather than obviously excessive. 

The investment requirement is not limited to upstream wells. It includes electricity, natural gas, pipelines, storage, ports, upgraders, environmental remediation, data systems, worker transportation, housing, security and domestic refining. Venezuela’s refineries were processing only approximately 31% of their nominal 1.29mb/d capacity in April 2026, forcing scarce light crudes and imported blendstocks to be allocated between domestic fuel production and heavy-crude dilution. 

DOES VENEZUELA NEED U.S. GOVERNMENT MONEY?

Direct U.S. taxpayer financing is not technically required. Private operators, service companies, infrastructure funds, commodity traders and project lenders could provide the capital if fiscal terms and legal protections are sufficient.

The U.S. government’s essential role would be enabling rather than operational. It would provide sanctions certainty, allow equipment and diluent exports, permit oil purchases, protect payment channels, establish acceptable dispute-resolution mechanisms and potentially facilitate political-risk mitigation.

Private capital will require priority cost recovery, control over operating budgets, transparent production measurement, reliable export rights, enforceable contracts and protection against future expropriation or sanctions reversal. Venezuela may therefore avoid direct public financing but would have to surrender part of the project economics and substantial operating control to attract private investment.

The statement that the transaction is “at no cost to the American taxpayer” does not mean there is no economic cost. The cost would be borne initially by private investors and recovered through crude entitlements, service fees, preferential purchase terms, production-sharing economics or field-level cash flow. The contractual details will determine how much value remains with Venezuela and how much is transferred to investors in exchange for capital and risk-bearing.

COULD CHINA, RUSSIA, EUROPE OR IRAN REPLACE THE U.S.?

Technically, much of the U.S. contribution could be replaced. Chinese companies can provide drilling rigs, pumps, pipelines, EPC services and financing. Russian companies possess heavy-oil and field-development experience. Iran has supplied diluent, refinery parts and technical assistance. European companies such as Eni, Repsol, Shell, BP and Maurel & Prom have experience in Venezuela and are included among entities currently authorized for certain Venezuelan oil and gas operations. 

However, a non-U.S. solution would probably be slower and more expensive under the present framework. The U.S. controls access to its own market and financial system, while U.S. sanctions affect shipping, insurance, banking and technology far beyond U.S. territory. Chinese and Russian companies have also previously demonstrated reluctance to commit unlimited new capital after payment problems, operational underperformance and contract disputes.

European companies can be important partners but generally have smaller existing oil-production platforms in Venezuela than Chevron and will require similar payment and legal protections. Iran can provide selected equipment and blendstocks but is unlikely to finance and execute a $50bn-$100bn industry reconstruction.

The optimal development model is consequently unlikely to be exclusively American or exclusively Venezuelan. A consortium structure involving Venezuelan personnel and state participation, U.S. and European operators, global service companies, commodity traders, infrastructure contractors and specialized financing would be more practical.

$VLO $MPC $PSX $DINO VENEZUELA/US RESERVE DEAL EXECUTIVE ASSESSMENT (1/x)

The announcement is strategically significant, but it should not yet be treated as a completed transfer of oil ownership, a bankable allocation of 65bn barrels to U.S. companies, or an immediate increase in global oil supply. The publicly available information establishes that the U.S. and Venezuela have negotiated a framework intended to give U.S. companies long-term access to Venezuelan fields and direct the resulting crude toward the U.S. market. It does not disclose the fields ultimately included, the companies receiving interests, the working-interest percentages, the production-sharing formula, royalties, taxes, cost-recovery provisions, capital commitments, reserve-booking rights, pricing arrangements, or the legal mechanism through which “majority U.S. control” would be exercised. Venezuelan officials are expected to execute field-level agreements, but the announcement remains materially under-specified from an investment-underwriting perspective. 

The central investment conclusion is that the near-term effect on PADD 3 refiners is positive, but the transmission mechanism is substantially narrower than the 65bn-barrel headline implies. The principal near-term benefit is additional access to heavy, high-sulfur crude; greater competition among heavy crude suppliers; improved crude-slate optionality; reduced reliance on longer-haul heavy grades; and potentially wider discounts for WCS, Maya and other competing barrels. The principal near-term effect is not a large increase in refinery throughput because PADD 3 is already operating near full capacity. May 2026 PADD 3 operable crude capacity was approximately 9.888mb/d and utilization was 96.9%, implying only approximately 0.31mb/d of arithmetic headroom before considering maintenance, unit constraints and crude-quality limitations. Most incremental Venezuelan barrels therefore displace other crude rather than create incremental runs. 

VLO and PSX represent the strongest direct public-equity beneficiaries among VLO, MPC, PSX and XOM. VLO has the highest refining purity, extensive capability to process high-acid Venezuelan heavy crude and management’s stated expectation that Venezuelan processing will exceed its historical maximum. PSX combines direct Venezuelan intake at Sweeny and Lake Charles with the strongest disclosed sensitivity to widening WTI-WCS differentials. MPC should benefit through its Garyville and Galveston Bay systems and through downward pressure on Canadian heavy prices, although management has stated that WCS is economically superior to Venezuelan crude in approximately 8 of 10 comparisons. XOM receives a downstream benefit but is the least direct equity expression because its integrated upstream exposure offsets part of the benefit from lower crude prices, its recent Beaumont expansion is oriented toward Permian crude, and it has not been publicly included in the current OFAC operating-license annex applicable to certain upstream operators. 

The gasoline-price claim is directionally plausible over a sufficiently long period but is overstated for the near term. The first barrels delivered under the framework are likely to increase refinery feedstock margins rather than immediately lower retail gasoline prices. Product prices are established in regional and global markets, while crude acquisition costs are specific to each refinery. When a complex Gulf Coast refiner substitutes a discounted Venezuelan barrel for a more expensive WCS, Maya or Middle Eastern heavy barrel, the initial economic benefit generally accrues to the refinery margin. Material consumer relief requires either enough incremental Venezuelan production to lower the global marginal crude price or sufficient incremental refinery product output to compress gasoline and distillate cracks. Neither outcome follows automatically from reallocating existing Venezuelan exports toward the U.S.

WHAT HAS ACTUALLY BEEN ANNOUNCED

The announcement states that the U.S. has secured “majority control” over more than 65bn barrels of Venezuelan proved reserves through a partnership with private business. Reuters reported that the framework followed several weeks of negotiations and is designed to lock in a group of Venezuelan oilfields for development by U.S. companies while guaranteeing the associated crude supply to the U.S. Reuters also reported that Venezuelan officials were preparing exploration and production agreements for execution, but that no fields, companies, transaction structure or control mechanism had been disclosed at the time of the announcement. 

The prior negotiating framework reportedly covered 17 fields, including mature acreage in the Lake Maracaibo region and undeveloped acreage in the Orinoco Belt. A lease model, followed by field-level tenders or auctions to U.S. producers, was under consideration. This distinction is important because mature Maracaibo assets and undeveloped Orinoco resources have radically different production profiles, capital requirements and time-to-market. Mature fields can produce incremental barrels through well workovers, artificial-lift restoration, water handling, compression and power-grid repairs, but frequently carry high decline rates and substantial integrity liabilities. Orinoco projects offer much larger resource scale but require new drilling, gathering systems, blending facilities, diluent supply, power, export infrastructure and, in some cases, upgrading capacity. 

The agreement should therefore be separated into 3 layers. The political layer is the 65bn-barrel statement. The regulatory layer is the sanctions, payments and licensing architecture already established by the U.S. Treasury. The commercial layer consists of field contracts, operating rights, fiscal terms and capital commitments that remain undisclosed. Only the regulatory layer is currently detailed enough to analyze with confidence. The commercial layer will determine whether U.S. companies receive economic ownership, operator control, production-sharing entitlements, service-fee economics, preferential offtake rights or some combination of these structures.

THE MEANING OF “MAJORITY U.S. CONTROL”

The most defensible interpretation is that “control” refers to contractual, operational, sanctions, payment and offtake control rather than U.S. sovereign ownership of Venezuelan hydrocarbons in the ground. OFAC General License 46D authorizes established U.S. entities to lift, buy, sell, transport, store and refine Venezuelan-origin oil for import into the U.S. Contracts with Venezuela or PDVSA must provide for dispute resolution in the U.S., U.K., France or Singapore, and relevant cash payments to blocked Venezuelan parties must be directed into Treasury-designated Foreign Government Deposit Funds. Shipping, insurance, port services and commercially reasonable crude, diluent and product swaps are also authorized. 

General License 52B broadly authorizes established U.S. entities to conduct transactions with PDVSA under similar payment and dispute-resolution requirements. However, it explicitly does not authorize the sale, transfer, assignment or pledge by the Venezuelan government of equity interests in PDVSA, PDVSA-controlled entities or other entities in which the Venezuelan government owns at least 50%. This restriction is inconsistent with interpreting the announcement as an outright transfer of PDVSA ownership or Venezuelan sovereign mineral title to the U.S. 

The January 2026 executive order governing the Foreign Government Deposit Funds is equally important. It states that the funds remain property of the Venezuelan government, are held by the U.S. solely in a custodial and governmental capacity, are not U.S. property and are protected from attachment by creditors. The U.S. therefore controls the payment channel and disposition process without claiming beneficial ownership of the money. The likely structure is analogous at the broader transaction level: Venezuelan sovereignty over the resource is retained, while the U.S. controls commercial participation, sanctioned counterparties, revenue custody, destination of production and dispute-resolution architecture. This is an inference from the published regulatory framework rather than a disclosed contract term. 

No basis presently exists to infer that “majority control” means U.S. companies will receive 51% of production, 51% of project cash flow, 51% of reserve ownership or 51% of field equity. Control rights and economic interests frequently differ. A company could operate a field and control capital programs while holding a minority economic interest. Conversely, a company could receive a large production entitlement without operating control. The field-level agreements must therefore be examined for working interest, cost recovery, profit-oil allocation, royalty burden, tax rates, domestic-supply obligations, export rights, abandonment liabilities and change-of-law protection before any valuation can be assigned.

THE 65BN-BARREL CLAIM

The latest EIA estimate places U.S. crude oil and lease condensate proved reserves at 46.0bn barrels at year-end 2024. Adding 65bn barrels arithmetically produces 111bn barrels, or 2.41x the domestic U.S. reserve figure. The 65bn-barrel amount is equivalent to 141% of existing U.S. proved reserves, so the statement that the transaction “more than doubles” U.S. reserves is mathematically correct only if a foreign sovereign resource under contractual access is added directly to the U.S. domestic reserve base. It is not correct as a geological, sovereign-inventory or public-company accounting characterization. 

The reserves are not part of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The SPR is a physical inventory of government-owned crude stored in salt caverns and was reported at approximately 290m barrels, or approximately 41% of capacity. Venezuelan oil in the ground is neither immediately available inventory nor an emergency stockpile. It must be produced, blended, transported, sold and refined. Conflating the 65bn barrels with the SPR materially overstates near-term energy security. 

The 65bn barrels also cannot automatically be booked by VLO, MPC, PSX, XOM or any upstream participant. SEC reserve recognition requires hydrocarbons to be economically and legally producible with reasonable certainty under existing operating, pricing, contractual, entitlement and regulatory conditions. Signed contracts, financing, infrastructure plans, field data, development approvals and legal rights are therefore necessary. A political allocation or memorandum does not by itself create SEC-bookable reserves. 

Venezuela has approximately 303bn barrels of proved crude reserves under country-level reporting, meaning 65bn barrels represent roughly 21.5% of the national total. A large proportion of Venezuela’s reserve base is extra-heavy Orinoco crude. These resources have materially lower economic value per barrel than light, infrastructure-connected barrels because they require diluent, specialized production systems, substantial surface facilities, high hydrogen consumption and complex refining. The appropriate valuation is the present value of after-tax entitlement cash flow after capital spending, operating costs, royalties, transportation, dilution, quality discounts and political risk, not the reserve volume multiplied by a benchmark oil price. 

The difference between reserves and flow is illustrated by simple arithmetic. Producing 65bn barrels at 1mb/d would require approximately 178 years. Producing the same amount at 2mb/d would require approximately 89 years. The investment value is therefore determined by the production plateau achievable during the first 10-20 years, not by the headline life of the resource. A project producing 100kb/d from a very large reserve base can be less valuable than a smaller field capable of reaching 300kb/d quickly with limited capital.

The reliability of the 65bn-barrel estimate also warrants scrutiny. Venezuela has not published routine comprehensive oil statistics for more than a decade, and the latest annual oil-ministry bulletin cited by Reuters dated to 2015. SLB has recently been contracted to organize and modernize PDVSA’s outdated and partially damaged reservoir and production databases, some of which reportedly must be reconstructed from paper records after server damage and a cyberattack. The data effort is evidence that field diligence, reserve reconciliation and production surveillance remain incomplete. The 65bn barrels should therefore be viewed as a sovereign resource allocation pending independent technical audit rather than as a fully diligenced reserve statement available for immediate corporate booking. 

The characterization of the arrangement as the “biggest oil deal in world history” cannot be evaluated without the economic interest conveyed. Reserve volume alone is not transaction value. A 65bn-barrel service contract earning a fixed fee per produced barrel would have a much lower NPV than a 65bn-barrel production-sharing interest with substantial profit-oil entitlement. A field concession with a high government take and large rehabilitation obligations could have limited value despite enormous resources. The transaction could ultimately become historically large, but the available disclosure does not yet establish that conclusion.

THE REGULATORY AND COMMERCIAL ARCHITECTURE

The U.S. has constructed a broad regulatory framework capable of supporting a controlled Venezuela-U.S. oil corridor. General License 46D covers crude lifting, marketing, purchase, transport, storage, insurance and refining. General License 47B permits U.S.-origin diluent exports to Venezuela. General License 48C authorizes U.S. goods, technology, software and services for exploration, development, production, electricity and repair activities. General License 52B authorizes broad transactions with PDVSA. Collectively, these licenses cover most of the physical chain required to send naphtha or condensate to Venezuela, produce and blend heavy crude, load it, insure it, transport it, import it and refine it in PADD 3. 

The framework is not equivalent to unrestricted commercial liberalization. General License 46D excludes transactions involving blocked vessels and specified Russian, Iranian, North Korean, Cuban and Chinese-controlled counterparties. General License 48C authorizes repair and oilfield support but does not itself authorize formation of new joint ventures or diluent exports. New field vehicles may therefore require separate authorization, qualification under another license or specific OFAC approval. 

General License 50C authorizes Venezuelan oil and gas operations for a named group consisting of BP, Chevron, Eni, Maurel & Prom, Repsol and Shell. Exxon Mobil is not included in the public annex as of August 27, 2026. This does not prevent XOM from importing or refining Venezuelan crude under the broader licenses, and it does not establish that XOM lacks a confidential specific license. It does mean that no public evidence currently exists that XOM has the same blanket upstream operating authorization as the listed companies. VLO, MPC and PSX should principally be analyzed as crude buyers and refiners unless separate production agreements are disclosed. 

The architecture gives Washington substantial control over counterparty selection, destination, cash custody, reporting and contract enforcement. It also reduces sanctions-evasion costs, tanker opacity and payment risk. Those improvements can support greater production and more reliable supply. They can simultaneously reduce the extreme sanctions discount previously embedded in Venezuelan barrels. A normalization of shipping, insurance and payment channels may increase Venezuela’s realized netback even while expanding availability. The refiner benefit therefore depends on the balance between increased volume and reduced discount.

The likely upstream structure is a lease, production-sharing contract, joint venture or operating-services arrangement under which a private company funds rehabilitation and development, controls field operations and receives production or cost recovery. Venezuela’s reformed legislation reportedly allows joint ventures and production-sharing contracts, but current regulation does not contain a conventional acreage-lease framework and the constitution reserves core petroleum activities to the state. Legal durability will therefore depend on how the contracts are approved, whether they are consistent with the constitution, and whether future Venezuelan governments recognize them. 

The “no cost to the American taxpayer” statement likely means that field capital would be supplied by private companies rather than through a direct federal appropriation. That does not establish that the arrangement has zero public cost or risk. Treasury administration, sanctions enforcement, diplomatic support, security policy and the ring-fencing of Venezuelan revenues are government functions. Any future federal guarantees, political-risk insurance, financing support, infrastructure aid or security commitments would represent direct or contingent public exposure. No complete cost structure has been disclosed.

PHYSICAL SUPPLY: CURRENT FLOWS AND THE REALISTIC RAMP

Venezuelan crude supply to the U.S. has already recovered substantially. Venezuela was producing approximately 1.25mb/d in August. July exports were approximately 1.16mb/d, of which approximately 786kb/d went to the U.S., up from 284kb/d in January. The U.S. therefore received approximately 68% of Venezuelan exports in July. Before the 2019 sanctions, U.S. Gulf Coast refineries processed approximately 800kb/d of Venezuelan crude. Current U.S. imports are already close to that historical level. This means the immediate economic significance of the new framework is more about making flows durable, direct and contractually secured than about creating an unprecedented near-term import surge. 

The first phase can increase U.S. access without increasing global supply. Existing cargoes can be redirected from India, Europe or Asia to PADD 3. That redirection is positive for U.S. refiners because it increases local heavy-crude availability and reduces freight distance, but it is largely neutral for the global crude balance. It may tighten competing heavy-crude supply in Asia and alter Middle Eastern heavy differentials without materially lowering Brent. Only incremental Venezuelan production, rather than geographic rerouting, directly expands world supply.

Near-term production increases are possible through additional diluent, workovers, pump replacements, electrical repairs, compression restoration, water-handling improvements and inventory liquidation. However, the export system is already a binding constraint. Venezuelan exports have struggled to exceed 1.25mb/d, tankers have experienced waits of up to 30 days, and delays have been attributed to aging infrastructure, power outages, crude-quality issues and slow loading. The Jose terminal handles approximately 70% of national exports, creating substantial concentration risk. A production increase that cannot be loaded does not create usable PADD 3 feedstock. 

Gross Venezuelan export numbers also overstate indigenous reservoir-liquid growth because extra-heavy crude must be blended with imported diluent. Venezuela imported approximately 81kb/d of heavy naphtha in July, while a U.S. energy official subsequently stated that more than 100kb/d of U.S. naphtha was being shipped to Venezuela. Part of the barrel returning to the Gulf Coast is therefore U.S.-origin diluent completing a round trip. The system can still create economic value through production enablement, marine transport and blending, but gross export growth should not be interpreted as an equal increase in Venezuelan-origin crude supply. 

A reasonable analytical framework contains 3 production phases. During the first 12 months, approximately 100-300kb/d of incremental production appears physically conceivable through workovers, inventory management, diluent availability and repair of existing facilities, but port and power constraints could prevent the full amount from reaching export markets. Over 1-4 years, approximately 300-800kb/d of incremental sustainable production may be achievable if contracts are bankable, service companies are paid, power and terminals are rehabilitated and sufficient drilling occurs. Restoring national production toward 2-3mb/d is a 5-10-year undertaking requiring very large capital deployment, extensive infrastructure rehabilitation, stable fiscal terms and continuous political support. These ranges are analytical scenarios rather than published forecasts.

The mix of the 17 fields will determine the slope of the ramp. Mature Maracaibo fields can deliver earlier barrels but often require intensive well intervention and carry high base declines, corrosion, water production and environmental liabilities. Greenfield Orinoco projects can provide large plateaus but require multi-year development and stable diluent economics. A portfolio containing more mature fields would be more relevant to 2027-2028 refinery feedstock economics. A portfolio dominated by undeveloped Orinoco acreage would be more relevant to long-duration upstream valuation than to near-term PADD 3 margins.

Secretary of State Rubio’s nearly $100bn private-investment estimate is consistent with the scale of the required reconstruction, but it does not establish that the capital has been committed or that acceptable returns are available. Private investment will depend on fiscal stability, cost-recovery priority, enforceability, access to foreign exchange, ability to repatriate cash, protection from legacy creditors and compensation for expropriation risk. 

PADD 3 REFINING ECONOMICS

PADD 3 is uniquely positioned to process Venezuelan crude because much of the region’s refinery fleet was designed or modified for heavy, high-sulfur, corrosive feedstocks. Beginning in the 1990s, Gulf Coast refiners expanded delayed-coking capacity and upgraded metallurgy to process Venezuelan, Mexican and Ecuadorian grades. Analysts estimate that the Gulf Coast can run approximately 3-4mb/d of heavy crude. At that throughput, every $1/bbl widening in the discount on heavy feedstocks represents approximately $1.1-$1.5bn of annual gross industry feedstock value before refinery-specific capture, crude substitutions, product-yield effects and higher operating costs. 

The core margin mechanism is the heavy-light differential. Product prices are largely set by regional and global gasoline, diesel and jet-fuel markets. A complex refinery capable of buying a cheaper heavy barrel while maintaining similar high-value product output captures the discount through coking, hydrocracking, catalytic cracking and hydrotreating. More Venezuelan supply should pressure competing heavy grades, including WCS, Maya, Colombian Castilla, Ecuadorian Napo, Basrah Heavy and certain Saudi grades. Even a refinery that purchases little Venezuelan crude can benefit if Venezuelan supply forces its incumbent suppliers to discount more aggressively.

The benefit is not equal to the quoted crude-price discount. Venezuelan crude frequently has low API gravity, high sulfur, metals, asphaltenes and, for certain grades, elevated total acid number. These characteristics increase desalter load, corrosion risk, catalyst consumption, hydrogen demand, sulfur-recovery load, petcoke production and maintenance requirements. The relevant economic comparison is the refinery-specific gross product worth less delivered crude cost, freight, demurrage, quality penalties, energy, hydrogen, catalyst and incremental maintenance. A nominally cheap barrel can be uneconomic if its quality exceeds refinery constraints.

The short voyage from Venezuela to the Gulf Coast generally reduces freight, transit time and working capital relative to Middle Eastern heavy crude. It may also create attractive backhaul economics because U.S. naphtha or condensate can move south as diluent while blended crude moves north. The current port congestion partly offsets that advantage. A tanker waiting 20-30 days can incur substantial demurrage and reduce effective fleet utilization. Crude contamination and quality disputes can add further cost. The value of the deal will therefore depend materially on terminal rehabilitation, tank integrity, blending consistency and loading reliability.

This Warsh presser was generally awful and a distraction.

(Bloomberg) -- For one day at least, bond traders got the message they were waiting for as Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warshdoubled down on his vow to finally tame inflation that’s outpaced the central bank’s target for five straight years.
The tone of his Jackson Hole, Wyoming, speech wasn’t new. But it was enough to dispel some of the doubts about the new Fed chief that this month helped drive long-dated Treasury yields to a nearly two decade high, pull down the US dollar and send investors rushing for rival havens like gold or Bitcoin. 

After Warsh spoke, two-year Treasury yields shot up by 12 basis points to 4.35%, the biggest jump since he struck a similarly hardline posture toward inflation in his first post-meeting press conference in June. 
Traders piled into bets that a quarter-point rate hike next month is more likely than not. The dollar rallied, gold dropped and 30-year yields were little changed — all signals that the Fed will act to cool inflation over time and, in so doing, keep long-term borrowing costs under control. 

“He came into this speech at Jackson Hole with the intention of rebuilding that credibility,” said Brian Quigley, who heads the US Treasuries team at Vanguard Group Inc. “You look at the market reaction, I think that was very effective.”
 
Alongside Nvidia Corp.’s earnings, Warsh’s appearance at the annual symposium was this week’s tone-setting event for global markets.

Yields had been steadily heading up ever since the US war on Iran hit the global economy with an energy-price shock earlier this year and the Fed continued to stick with its wait-and-see stance. But after 30-year yields hit the highest levels since 2007, that started raising renewed concerns and exerting a drag on stock prices in the wake of the recent record-setting run.
Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent made an unusual effort to stop yields from rising by announcing plans to buy back more bonds, which fanned fears that Washington was looking to artificially cap longer-term rates without addressing the inflation and yawning budget deficit that have been pushing them higher.
Warsh also contributed to the market’s selloff. When the Fed held rates steady again in July — despite his hawkish tone a month earlier — long-term bond yields jumped sharply as traders demanded higher payouts in return for the risk of heightened inflation. Some of his comments, including questioning whether the Fed’s preferred price gauge remains the right target, added to doubts about his commitment to price stability.

On Friday, he moved to allay those worries. He made no effort to downplay the inflation figures this week that showed it was running at 3.7%, saying underlying trends haven’t “meaningfully improved.” He said he considers the Fed’s 2% target as “firm and fixed.” And while he has broken from his predecessors’ practice of providing guidance on where rates are heading, he said the Fed needs to ensure that inflation is receeding back to that level “at sufficient speed.”
